units: metres; x east, y north; level = storey, 4 m each
rule: Ask what happens to the weights, and you know where you are: before the house (garden), being learned (below ground), used once (ground floor), changed after training (first floor), frozen while the words change (second floor), scored by the world (yard), read only (tower).

objects.idea: The perceptron rule: on each mistake, add the point to the weights if its label is +1 and subtract it if −1; a right answer changes nothing.
objects.image: A garden rake on a string line lunges at every plant on the wrong side and drags the string toward it, then rests.

card.title: Nudge the line at each mistake
card.text: The perceptron scores a point x by w·x and predicts its sign. Add a constant 1 to every point and the bias becomes one more weight. On a mistake, add y·x to the weights, where y is the label, +1 or −1. Points it already gets right change nothing, and there is no learning rate.
card.formula: w ← w + y·x   (on each mistake)
card.measured: 12 mistakes in 3 epochs (11, 1, 0), then 100% accuracy: 200 separable points, seed 1958, module 00a.

objects.checked: README Goals, What you'll see (the perceptron), This module's numbers table; python/run_perceptron.json (mistakes 12, per_epoch [11,1,0], accuracy 1.0); Zig lane paragraph (no learning rate, starts from w = 0).

objects.idea: If some line splits the data with margin γ, and every point lies within radius R, the perceptron makes at most (R/γ)² mistakes, then stops.
objects.image: A tally post with only so many notches: the wider the gap between the two dashed strings, the fewer the notches, and the rake must stop when they run out.

card.title: It always stops
card.text: The margin γ is the smallest distance from any point to a line that splits the data; R is the largest distance from a point to the origin; both are measured after the constant 1 is added to each point. Each mistake moves w at least γ further along that line's direction, while its squared length grows by at most R². Both cannot go on forever, so the mistakes run out. The bound is a worst case: real runs use a small part of it.
card.formula: mistakes ≤ (R/γ)²
card.measured: Bound 139.57; the run made 12, 8.60% of it: R = 4.169359, γ = 0.352921, module 00a.

objects.checked: README Theory in one minute (proof, u·w ≥ mγ, ‖w‖ ≤ R√m), This module's numbers (R, γ, bound 139.57, 8.60%), margin sweep paragraph (6 to 47 mistakes at margin 0.07; run_margin_sweep.json mistakes_min 6, max 47).

objects.idea: Least squares is a projection: the fit is the point of the columns' span closest to the targets, and the residual meets every column at a right angle.
objects.image: A sundial: the shadow is the fit, the upright pin the residual. A ball hopping toward the shadow's tip lands on it; make each hop too long and it bounds off the dial.

card.title: The fit is a shadow
card.text: Least squares picks the weights whose predictions lie closest to the targets. The predictions can only be mixes of the feature columns, so the best fit is the foot of a perpendicular from the targets onto the space those columns span, and the residual meets every column at a right angle. Gradient descent walks to the same point, but only while its step stays below 2/λ_max, where λ_max is the largest eigenvalue of the loss's curvature 2XᵀX/n. Past that edge each step overshoots further than the last.
card.formula: Xᵀ(y − Xw) = 0   ·   stable when η < 2/λ_max
card.measured: Solved and walked answers agree to 1.8e−15 (400 steps, rate 0.05); residual orthogonal to 1.5e−13; edge 2/λ_max = 0.343976: 40 points, module 00a.

objects.checked: README Goals (two ways, projection), Least squares is a right angle, The same answer walked to, This module's numbers; python/src/perceptron/lstsq.py (loss = ‖Xw−y‖²/n, H = 2XᵀX/n, edge 2/λ_max); run_least_squares.json (n 40, max_abs_diff 1.78e−15, orthogonality 1.51e−13, stability_edge 0.34398). P.sundial captions 'target y', 'fit Xw', 'step below the bound: settles', 'step past the bound: flies off' are correct.

objects.idea: No line splits XOR, so the perceptron cycles forever; one hidden layer of two tanh units bends the plane until a line works again.
objects.image: Four beds in a checker of blue and gold; the string spins forever until the bed folds like a cloth and the string lies flat between.

card.title: Bend the plane, then cut
card.text: XOR puts one class on two opposite corners of a square and the other class on the remaining two. Any line gets at least one corner wrong, so the perceptron never settles: its weights return to where they started every four updates. A hidden layer of two tanh units gives each point new coordinates, and in them a line splits the classes. Gradient descent finds those weights.
card.measured: Best line: 75% of the 4 points; 2 → 2 → 1 tanh network: 9 parameters, 4 of 4 right, loss 2.5e−32. Module 00a.

objects.checked: README The wall, Goals (XOR), This module's numbers (75%, 9 parameters, 4/4, 2.5e−32); run_xor.json (perceptron per_epoch 4 mistakes every epoch, mlp hidden 2, n_params 9, loss_final 2.47e−32). Formation xor() folds y → 1.7·x·y so class with x·y > 0 rises; cut y = 0: consistent.

also.idea: Ridge adds a penalty on the size of the weights, (XᵀX + λI)w = Xᵀy, so two near-copy features stop cancelling in huge opposite weights.
also.image: Two stakes pulling the string in opposite directions with all their might, until a spring between them makes both relax.

card.title: Keep the weights small
card.text: Add a near-copy of one feature and the normal equations give two huge weights that cancel. Ridge adds λ times the squared size of the weights to the loss, so cancelling giants cost more than they gain, and the fit picks small weights. Training error barely moves.

objects.idea: Bayes in odds: posterior odds are prior odds times the likelihood ratio, so a test right 96% of the time on the sick can leave you 95% likely to be healthy.
objects.image: A hive with one queen among thousands of bees; a sieve catches the queen and a crowd of workers, and the workers win.

card.title: Rare things fool good tests
card.text: Bayes' rule turns a prior into a posterior. In odds it is one multiplication: the odds before times the likelihood ratio, sensitivity divided by the false-positive rate. Here that ratio is 12, but the odds before are 1 to 249, so false positives outnumber true ones about twenty to one. The numbers are a made-up worked example.
card.formula: odds after = odds before × sensitivity / (1 − specificity)
card.measured: P(ill | positive) = 4.598%: prevalence 0.4%, sensitivity 96%, specificity 92%, module 00b.

objects.checked: README Goals, Part 1 (worked example, 0.045977, 3.84 vs 79.68, LR+ = 12, 1:249, table 4.598%, caveat on independence). F.rare captions '1,000 people', '4 sick', 'flagged but healthy', '4.6% of flags are sick' are right.

objects.idea: k-NN labels a point by a vote of its k nearest neighbours; as data grows, 1-NN's error ends between the Bayes error and about twice it.
objects.image: A newcomer on a bench turns to the seven nearest trees and takes their vote; two fences beside the bench mark the Bayes error and twice it.

card.title: Ask the neighbours
card.text: k-NN stores the training set and labels a new point by a vote of its k nearest points; nothing is trained. At k = 1 training error is zero and test error is worst: that is overfitting. Larger k averages more labels. When classes overlap even the best rule errs, and that floor is the Bayes error; with enough data, 1-NN lands at most about twice it.
card.formula: R* ≤ lim R_1NN ≤ 2R*(1 − R*)
card.measured: Test error 0.2274 at k = 1 and 0.1593 at k = 151, against a best possible 0.158655; 1-NN settles near 0.222–0.225 under a ceiling of 0.266968. Module 00b.

objects.checked: README Part 3 (error vs k table, R* = 0.158655, Cover-Hart table and bound, 1-NN row 0.2218–0.2245). F.knn uses the 7 nearest points (arr[6]), matching 'seven'.

objects.idea: PCA by power iteration: multiply any arrow by the covariance again and again and it turns to the main axis; subtract that axis to find the next.
objects.image: A weather vane that, each time the wind blows, swings closer to the orchard's long row.

card.title: Find the direction that matters
card.text: The covariance matrix C records how the data's coordinates vary together. Multiplying a vector by C stretches it most along the direction of greatest spread, so repeating and rescaling leaves only that direction: the first principal component. Its error shrinks by λ₂/λ₁ each step. Subtract λ₁u₁u₁ᵀ from C and repeat to find the next one.
card.formula: v ← C·v / ‖C·v‖
card.measured: PC1 holds 28.68% of FashionMNIST's pixel variance; 83 of 784 components hold 90%. Module 00b.

objects.checked: README Part 4 (power iteration, gap ratio, deflation C ← C − λ₁u₁u₁ᵀ, components table 83 for 90%, PC1 28.68%). F.pca draws a 30° cloud, matching the module's 2-D demo; no captions.

objects.idea: k-means sums a cloud up with a few centres: send each point to its nearest centre, move each centre to its points' mean, repeat until nothing moves.
objects.image: Three scarecrows that each walk to the middle of the birds they scare, until none moves.

card.title: Centres walk to their points
card.text: k-means places k centres. Assign each point to its nearest centre, move each centre to the mean of its points, and repeat. Neither step can raise the mean squared distance, so the run stops, but where it stops depends on the start. A moving average over small batches adds noise that can shake a centre out of a poor spot, if the noise is strong enough.
card.formula: error = (1/n) Σᵢ ‖xᵢ − c_a(i)‖²
card.measured: Means 5 apart, k = 4, 300 starts: Lloyd ends stuck on 55.3%, the moving average (batch 256) on 32.7%. Module 00b.

objects.checked: README Part 5 (Lloyd's two steps, 'neither step can raise the error', where it stops depends on the start, moving-average rule, results table gap 5: 55.3% / 32.7%, gap 6 batch 32: 11.3%). P.kmeans caption 'round n' is fine.

also.idea: Naive Bayes assumes the features are independent once the class is known: closed form and cheap, but it cannot follow features that move together.
also.image: Garden gnomes who each vote on the flower alone, never looking at one another.

card.title: Each feature votes alone
card.text: Naive Bayes models each class with one bell curve per feature and multiplies them, as if the features were independent given the class. Fitting it is one pass of means and variances. On tilted clouds its axis-aligned cut cannot follow the tilt: 0.8320 accuracy against 0.8930 with full covariance.

also.checked: README Part 2 (naive assumption, one pass of .mean() and .var(), 2-D table 0.8320 vs 0.8930, Pullover vs Coat 0.7225 vs 0.8590).

objects.idea: The hard-margin SVM finds the line with the widest empty band; only the points on the band's edge, the support vectors, get a weight α above zero.
objects.image: A plank laid across the pond as wide as it will go, held up by three stones that touch its edges; the rest of the stones could vanish.

card.title: The widest plank
card.text: A perceptron stops at the first line that works. A hard-margin support vector machine picks the line with the widest empty band between the classes. In its dual form the answer is a weighted sum of training points, and only points on the band's edge get a weight α above zero. Those are the support vectors: delete any other point and the line does not move.
card.formula: w = Σ αᵢ yᵢ xᵢ   (αᵢ > 0 only on the margin)
card.measured: 3 support vectors of 24 points; band width 2/‖w‖ = 1.462661. Module 00c.

objects.checked: README Part 1 (primal, dual, w = Σαᵢyᵢxᵢ, complementary slackness, 3 of 24, band 1.462661).

objects.idea: The kernel trick: lift the points so a flat cut works, and get inner products in the lifted space straight from the original points, never building the lift.
objects.image: Two rings of lily pads; a swell lifts the outer ring high and the inner one hardly at all, and a flat sheet of glass slides between them.

card.title: Lift, then cut flat
card.text: Two rings, one inside the other, cannot be split by a line. Give each point a height x² + y² and the outer ring rises above the inner one, so a flat plane splits them. The SVM's dual uses the data only through inner products, so any kernel k(a, b) that equals an inner product after some lift can replace them, and the lift is never built. The picture's lift belongs to the kernel aᵀb + ‖a‖²‖b‖²; the module's quadratic kernel (aᵀb)² uses (x₁², √2·x₁x₂, x₂²).
card.formula: k(a, b) = φ(a)·φ(b)
card.measured: Quadratic kernel on 120 ring points: 4 support vectors, identity checked to 1.07e−14; the RBF kernel needs 13. Module 00c.

objects.checked: README Part 2 (inner-product-only data, φ for (aᵀb)², 1.07e−14, 120 points, 4 SVs, picture-book map belongs to aᵀb + ‖a‖²‖b‖², RBF 13 SVs). P.lift captions 'no line splits two rings', 'height = x² + y²', 'a flat cut' are correct for the picture-book lift.

objects.idea: A Hopfield network stores patterns as valleys of an energy; one-unit updates never go uphill, so a damaged pattern rolls back to the stored one.
objects.image: A stone basin carved with hollows; a chipped marble dropped in rolls into the nearest hollow and comes out whole.

card.title: Memories are valleys
card.text: A Hopfield network stores patterns by adding up their outer products; nothing is trained. Updating one unit at a time never raises the energy, so a damaged input rolls downhill and most often stops in the stored pattern it came from. Store too many and spurious valleys swallow the real ones. In very large networks that happens near 0.138 patterns per unit; small ones hold a little more.
card.formula: E = −½ sᵀWs,   W = (1/N) Σ ξξᵀ, diagonal 0
card.measured: Five letters in 100 neurons, 30% of bits destroyed: all five recovered. Measured capacity 0.1950 per unit at N = 100, 0.1528 at N = 1,600. Module 00c.

objects.checked: README Part 3 (storage rule, E = −½sᵀWs, E never goes up, five letters 30%, capacity table, 0.138 as N → ∞, spurious valleys swallow real ones).

objects.idea: Double descent: test error spikes where parameters equal data points, then falls again as the fitter picks the smallest-norm fit; here it never gets back below the first dip.
objects.image: A footbridge dips, climbs to a sharp hump at the pond's neck, then comes down again, but lands higher than its first dip.

card.title: The curve that dips twice
card.text: Fit polynomials to 20 noisy points. Test error falls, then rises, as the textbook says. At degree 19 there are 20 coefficients, one per point, and exactly one curve fits them all, with huge coefficients. Past that, many curves fit, the pseudo-inverse picks the one with the smallest coefficients, and test error falls again. Here the second dip stays above the first.
card.measured: Test error 0.0183 at degree 3, 1.11e+12 at degree 19, 0.4825 at degree 47; coefficient length 1.26e+06 at degree 19, 0.70 at degree 80. Module 00c.

objects.checked: README Part 5 (bias² 0.0032 + variance 0.0088 at degree 3, table of test MSE, ‖β‖ values, training error 2.07e−18, honest note, Curth et al. in Where this shows up later). F.dd data DDT matches the table; caption 'degree 19: as many weights as points' correct (20 coefficients, 20 points); 'floor' captions '0.0183 at degree 3', '0.4825 at degree 47' correct.

also.idea: The modern Hopfield update Xᵀsoftmax(βXξ) lines up term by term with attention, softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V.
also.image: A torch from the atrium stands by the basin: shine it on the hollows and the best match flashes back, the same trick as the mirrors indoors.

card.title: Lookup is a dot product
card.text: Replace the sign in the Hopfield update with a softmax and one step scores every stored pattern against the probe and blends them. That is attention: the probe is the query, the stored patterns are keys and values, and β plays 1/√d. The softmax rule holds 10,000 patterns in 100 neurons, where the classic rule recalls only 20% of 20.

also.checked: README Part 4 (update rule, line-up table, capacity table: classical 0.56 at 15, 0.20 at 20; modern 1.00 up to 10,000, 0.88 at 20,000).

objects.idea: Every operation you apply records a node with its inputs; running the expression forward builds a graph.
objects.image: Every word you say in the echo room is carved as a stone on the floor, joined by string to the words it came from.

card.title: The forward pass leaves a trail
card.text: The engine's Value type records every +, *, tanh, exp, pow and relu you apply, with links to its inputs. Running an expression forward builds a directed acyclic graph, a graph whose arrows never loop back. Each node holds its value, and after backward() its gradient.

objects.checked: README intro (Value records +, *, tanh, exp, pow, relu), Theory in one minute (DAG definition, forward value, gradient).

objects.idea: Backpropagation is message passing: in reverse order, each node multiplies the slope it receives by its own local slope and adds the result into its inputs.
objects.image: Shout at the last stone and the echo runs back along the strings, louder or softer at each stone.

card.title: Send the slope backwards
card.text: Each operation knows its local derivative: how its output moves when its input moves. Backward starts with slope 1 at the output and walks the graph in reverse topological order, so every node has heard from all the nodes that used it before it passes anything on. Each node multiplies what it received by its local derivative and adds the result into its inputs.
card.formula: slope at input += slope at output × local derivative
card.measured: tanh neuron with o = 0.7071: local slope 1 − o² = 0.5; gradient at x1 = −1.5, at w1 = 1.0. Module 01.

objects.checked: README Theory in one minute (one rule, reverse topological order, worked neuron and its gradients), Goals (message passing, topological sort).

objects.idea: Gradient checking: compare each slope from backward() with a finite difference, nudging the input both ways, to catch a wrong derivative.
objects.image: A pair of scales by the door weighs every slope against a nudge of the input; a wrong one tips over.

card.title: Weigh every slope
card.text: Nudge one input by a tiny ε each way and measure how much the output moves. That needs no calculus, so it checks backward() independently. If one op's local derivative is wrong, its slopes disagree with the nudge, and the check points at it.
card.formula: slope ≈ (f(x + ε) − f(x − ε)) / 2ε
card.measured: backward() and finite differences agree to about 1e−10. Module 01.

objects.checked: README What you'll see (gradient check ~1e-10), Hands-on (central difference formula), Exercises 3 (buggy_engine.py: find the wrong op), Goals.

objects.idea: With this engine a small network walks downhill on its loss and classifies two moons' 100 training points with 100% accuracy.
objects.image: A ball rolls down the floor of the echo room into a bowl, step by step against the slope.

card.title: Then walk downhill
card.text: The gradient lists the loss's slope for every weight and points uphill. Gradient descent subtracts a small multiple of it and repeats. Here a 2 → 16 → 16 → 1 network with a hinge loss, max(0, 1 − y·score), learns to split two interleaving moons. There is no held-out set yet; module 02 adds one.
card.formula: w ← w − η·∇L(w)
card.measured: 100% accuracy on the 100 training points of make_moons. Module 01.

objects.checked: README intro (100% on 100 training points, no held-out set), Hands-on (hinge loss), Zig lane (Python net 2→16→16→1); scripts/train_moons.py (hinge loss, p.data -= lr * p.grad).

also.idea: Run backward in reverse topological order, so each node has all its gradient before it passes any on.
also.image: Numbered stepping stones; the echo may only leave a stone once every string into it has rung.

card.title: Order the echo
card.text: A topological sort lists the nodes so each comes after every node it reads from. Walked backwards, that list visits every consumer before its producer, so a node's gradient is complete before it passes messages on. One backward pass then gives every slope.

also.checked: README Theory in one minute (two terms: DAG, topological sort; reverse order), Goals, Checkpoint.

objects.idea: A network is weighted sums, each followed by a bend; you derive each layer's forward and backward pass by hand.
objects.image: The mill's stacked grindstones, each one tilted, each one followed by a hinge.

card.title: Layers, by hand
card.text: A Linear layer computes y = xW + b; ReLU keeps positive values and sets negative ones to zero. Each layer caches what it needs on the way forward. On the way back it takes the gradient of its output and returns the gradient of its input and of its weights. Stack them and you have the network.
card.formula: dL/dW = xᵀg,  dL/db = Σg,  dL/dx = gWᵀ;   ReLU: dL/dx = g·[x > 0]
card.measured: 0.8646 accuracy on all 10,000 test images: 784 → 256 → 10, NumPy, backward written by hand. Module 02.

objects.checked: README Theory (forward chain, Linear and ReLU gradients), Hands-on output (FINAL TEST ACCURACY 0.8646); results/fashion.json test_acc 0.8646.

objects.idea: Fuse softmax with cross-entropy and the gradient on the scores is just the predicted probabilities minus the one-hot answer.
objects.image: A row of sacks on a scale; the right sack is pulled down by exactly how short it fell.

card.title: Probabilities minus the answer
card.text: The last layer gives one raw score per class, the logits; softmax turns them into probabilities that sum to 1. Cross-entropy charges minus the log of the true class's probability. Take the two together and the gradient on the logits is the probabilities minus the one-hot answer, divided by the batch size. You derive it in exercise (a) and check it against finite differences.
card.formula: dL/d(logits) = (softmax − onehot) / N
card.measured: All three layers pass a finite-difference check: max relative error 5e−10 on a 5 → 7 → 6 → 3 network. Module 02.

objects.checked: README Theory (logits, fused gradient, onehot, N = batch size, gradcheck 5e-10), Exercises (a).

objects.idea: It overfits: training loss keeps falling while validation loss bottoms out and wanders up; early stopping keeps the weights from its lowest point.
objects.image: Two water marks on the mill wall: one keeps sinking, the other bottoms out and starts to rise.

card.title: Two curves tell it
card.text: Hold back part of the data as a validation set and score it after every epoch, one pass over the training set. Training loss keeps falling because the net sees the same images again and again. Validation loss stops improving once the net learns details of the training images that do not carry over. Early stopping keeps the weights from the epoch with the lowest validation loss; this module did not stop early.
card.measured: Validation loss lowest at epoch 17 (0.360, accuracy 0.877); at epoch 25 train loss 0.216, validation 0.411; 18,000 training images. Module 02.

also.idea: The training loop: split once, then every epoch shuffle, and for each mini-batch run forward, loss, backward and a step; measure at the end of the epoch.
also.image: A waterwheel with six buckets, each painted with one step, turning round and round.

card.title: The loop turns the wheel
card.text: Split the data once into training and validation. Each epoch, shuffle the training set; for each mini-batch, run forward, compute the loss, run backward and let the optimizer step. After the epoch, measure loss and accuracy on both sets. The room's waterwheel is this loop.

objects.idea: Make deterministic, disjoint train, validation and test splits, by whatever unit could leak; let the test set shape no choice and open it once.
objects.image: Three locked chests; the test chest has one key, which breaks in the lock after one use.

card.title: Hold some data back
card.text: The training split fits the weights. The validation split makes the choices: which threshold, when to stop. The test split gives the final estimate and must shape no choice at all. When examples come in groups, such as several samples from one person, split by the group, not by the row.

objects.idea: The confusion matrix is the primitive: accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1 all come from its four counts.
objects.image: Four drawers in the vault, labelled by the two ways to be right and the two ways to be wrong.

card.title: Four counts behind every score
card.text: A threshold turns each predicted probability into yes or no, and each example lands in one of four cells: true or false, positive or negative. Precision asks how many yes answers were right; recall asks how many true cases were caught; F1 combines the two. Accuracy misleads when positives are rare: always saying no is 99% accurate when 1% are positive.
card.formula: precision = TP/(TP+FP),  recall = TP/(TP+FN),  F1 = 2·P·R/(P+R)
card.measured: At threshold 0.5 on all 160 rows: precision 0.810, recall 0.780, F1 0.795. Module 05a.

objects.checked: README The confusion matrix is the primitive (four cells, formulas, 99% example); results/evaluation_lab.json sweep_all_rows 0.50.

objects.idea: A threshold is a product decision: moving it trades missed positives for false alarms, so choose it on validation data and freeze it.
objects.image: A sliding bar across the vault door; push it and coins fall from one drawer into the other.

card.title: Move the threshold, move the errors
card.text: Lowering the threshold catches more positives and raises more false alarms; raising it does the reverse. The right place depends on what each error costs: a screening test favours recall, an alert that interrupts people favours precision. Pick it on validation data, freeze it, then score the test set once.

card.title: A leak makes a fake win
card.text: Exact duplicates across a split are easy to find by ID or by hashing the content. Near-copies, several samples from one person and leaks across time are harder. MinHash, a cheap estimate of how many word n-grams two texts share, finds near-copies at scale. Removing leaked examples can make a good score fall, which shows how much of it was the leak.

also.image: A shelf of jars labelled 10% to 90%, each filled to how often it was right; the honest jars match their labels.

card.title: Does 80% sure mean 80% right?
card.text: Calibration asks whether predictions made with confidence p come true about p of the time. Expected calibration error bins predictions by confidence, compares each bin's mean predicted probability with the share of its examples that were positive, and averages the gaps, weighted by bin size. Its value depends on the bins and the sample size, so report both. The lab's model scores 0.0657 with 10 bins.

card.title: Gaps need error bars
card.text: A slice is a subgroup, such as photos taken in low light; it has fewer examples, so its score is noisier. The bootstrap resamples a slice's examples with replacement 2,000 times and keeps the middle 95% of the scores. objects.idea: Three update rules: plain gradient descent steps down the slope; momentum adds up past steps, so steps that agree speed up; Adam scales each weight's step by its recent gradients.
objects.image: Three balls race down the curved floor: one plods, one swings and gathers speed, one changes its stride on every tile.

card.title: Three ways downhill
card.text: Gradient descent steps against the gradient. Momentum keeps a running sum of past gradients: steps that agree add up, steps that flip sign cancel. Adam divides each weight's step by the size of its recent gradients, so every weight moves at about the same pace. In Rosenbrock's curved valley, momentum and Adam needed about 20 times fewer steps than gradient descent.
card.formula: momentum: v ← 0.9·v + g;  p ← p − lr·v
card.measured: Steps to loss below 10⁻³ in Rosenbrock's valley, each at its best rate: gradient descent 3,660, momentum 164, Adam 182 (module 14, section 1).

objects.idea: The learning rate decides a lot: too large and the steps overshoot and grow, and each optimiser has its own best rate.
objects.image: A ball thrown too hard bounces from wall to wall of the slope, each bounce higher, and never settles.

card.title: Step size decides a lot
card.text: On the tilted bowl, whose largest curvature is 25, gradient descent diverged at every rate from 0.1 up; the limit is 2/25 = 0.08. Adam diverged at none of its 37 rates. On module 02's network the best rate was 0.3 for SGD, 0.03 for momentum and 0.003 for Adam, and Adam at 0.3 ended at 19 to 22%. So compare optimisers each at its own best rate.

objects.idea: Measure how sharp a valley is by its top Hessian eigenvalue: here the large-batch net sat in a valley 16 times sharper, yet tested better.
objects.image: Two balls roll into two valleys of the floor, one narrow, one wide; a surveyor slices the floor across each and holds up a sharp V and a wide U.

card.title: Sharp is not always worse
card.text: The top eigenvalue of the Hessian, the matrix of second derivatives, is the curvature along the direction in which the loss bends most. Power iteration finds it from Hessian-vector products, without building the Hessian. Slices along filter-normalised random directions show the same shape. Here sharpness alone did not predict test accuracy, and the eigenvalue changes when the same function is written with rescaled weights.
card.formula: Hv by two gradient passes; power iteration: v ← Hv / ‖Hv‖
card.measured: Batch 2,048: top eigenvalue 35.2, test accuracy 86.2%; batch 32: 2.2 and 84.8%. One pair of runs (module 14, section 3).

objects.idea: A network can fit its training set long before it finds the rule; in this run, weight decay decided whether the late jump came at all.
objects.image: A clock on the far wall shows the wrong time for hours, then suddenly the right one; a small weight on its pendulum, pulling it back each swing, is what does it.

card.title: Fit first, understand later
card.text: A one-layer transformer learns (a + b) mod 97 from 30% of all pairs. With weight decay 1.0 it fits its training pairs by step 130, but scores 95% on the other pairs only at step 5,900, about 45 times later. With no weight decay, test accuracy was 4.5% after 20,000 steps. Weight decay shrinks every weight a little each step; one reading is that it pushes toward the small weights that compute the sum. Two runs cannot prove that reading.
card.formula: AdamW decay: w ← w − lr·wd·w, beside the gradient step
card.measured: Train accuracy 100% at step 130 (wd 1.0) and 120 (wd 0); test ≥ 95% at step 5,900 with wd 1.0, not within 20,000 steps with wd 0; weight norm 36.7 → 57.2 → 32.2 with decay, 80.6 and rising without (module 14, section 4).

also.image: A dimmer switch on the wall that brightens in a straight line, then fades along a smooth curve to dark.

card.title: Warm up, then fade
card.text: The rate climbs from 0 to its base value over the first 10% of steps, then falls to 0 along half a cosine. At each optimiser's best rate it beat a constant rate for SGD and Adam on all three seeds, and shrank the spread between seeds to 0.1 to 0.3 points. At small rates it hurt. transformers ships the same schedule as get_cosine_schedule_with_warmup.

objects.idea: A self-supervised objective makes its own targets from the input: hide part and predict it back, either its pixels or its latent, the encoder's summary of it.
objects.image: Blindfolded statues trace with their hands the half of the picture that is covered; one draws the missing pixels, another only names what is there.

card.title: Hide part, predict it
card.text: Masked reconstruction hides 60% of the image's 64 patches, each 4 × 4 pixels, and redraws their pixels. I-JEPA-lite hides four blocks and predicts, cell by cell, what a slow moving copy of the encoder outputs for them: latents, not pixels. No label is read while the encoder trains. A linear probe on the frozen encoder then measures what it kept, against a random encoder as the floor.
card.measured: Class probe, 10,000 training images: random weights 40.1%, masked reconstruction 45.2%, I-JEPA-lite 47.9%, supervised 82.5% (CIFAR-10, 250 s of training each, none for the random one; module 16, section 1).

objects.checked: README §1: definition of self-supervised, MAE (60% of 64 patches of 4 × 4), I-JEPA-lite (four rectangles, 15–20%, EMA target 0.996→1.0, 'compares latents, not pixels'), probe table and floor/ceiling.

objects.idea: Or match two views: two random crops of one image should land close together, and far from the views of every other image in the batch.
objects.image: Two halves of one torn photo pulled together across the room by a spring, while the other photos are pushed away.

card.title: Match two views
card.text: The contrastive method SimCLR makes two views of each image by random crop, flip, colour jitter and sometimes grey. Its loss asks each view to pick its partner out of the other 2B − 1 views in the batch, by cosine similarity over a temperature. A random encoder already probes at 40.1%, so judge each method by its gain over that floor.
card.formula: NT-Xent: cross-entropy over cosine similarities / τ, τ = 0.2
card.measured: Class probe 57.9%, against 40.1% for the random encoder and 82.5% for the supervised one (CIFAR-10, 10,000 probe images, module 16).

objects.idea: Collapse: map every input to one point and a JEPA loss is zero, and the encoder has learned nothing.
objects.image: All the statues turn and point at the same nail in the wall.

card.title: The cheat: one point for all
card.text: A JEPA loss compares two outputs of the same encoder, so it is zero when every input maps to one point. A milder form, dimensional collapse, keeps outputs apart but along a few directions only. Two meters: the spread of the normalised outputs, and the effective rank, the number of directions that carry variance. Each misses a case: the collapsed run had the highest effective rank.
card.measured: Without stop-grad, the spread fell from 0.16 to 0.005 and the prediction loss to 0.0005 within six seconds; the effective rank dipped, then climbed back, and read 17.8 after 120 seconds (module 16, section 2).

objects.checked: README §2: definition of collapse and dimensional collapse, two meters, table (no stop-grad 0.0015 std, rank 17.8, probe 38.1%), 'Within six seconds ... 0.16 to 0.005 ... 0.0005'. a48 deeper matches.

objects.idea: Block collapse four ways: stop the gradient, use a slow moving copy as target, add a variance term, or push outputs toward a Gaussian; only a labelled probe told the runs apart.
objects.image: A sheepdog runs round the points and keeps them spread in a round flock, yet the widest flock is not the one that knows the most.

card.title: Make spread a rule
card.text: Four guards were tried for 120 seconds each: stop-grad, an EMA target, VICReg's variance term, and SIGReg, which pushes outputs toward a standard Gaussian. Each kept the outputs from shrinking to a point. Only the EMA target probed above the random floor. Picked by spread or effective rank alone, the wrong runs would have won.
card.measured: Class probe: EMA 44.8% against the 40.1% floor; SIGReg spread widest, 0.968, but probed 22.1%; variance term alone: effective rank 1.0 (module 16, section 2).

also.idea: A JEPA predicts the latent of each hidden block, what a slow copy of the encoder outputs for it, not its pixels.
also.image: A statue points at a sealed box and names what it holds, without ever drawing it.

card.title: Predict the summary, not the pixels
card.text: I-JEPA-lite hides four blocks of the 8 × 8 grid. A predictor guesses, cell by cell, what a second encoder outputs for the hidden cells of the full image. The second encoder is a slow moving average of the first and gets no gradient. Pixel losses keep what varies most, like mean colour; masked reconstruction kept mean colour best (R² 0.987).

objects.idea: Backprop keeps every layer's input until the backward pass comes back down, so its memory grows with depth and with batch size.
objects.image: A porter climbs the stairs leaving a copy of every room he passes on the landing, then walks back down collecting them.

card.title: What backprop keeps
card.text: To get the gradient of a layer's weights, backprop needs that layer's input, so the forward pass keeps one batch × width matrix per layer. Add one gradient per weight and, for Adam, two running averages per weight. Inference needs none of this. Checkpointing keeps only some inputs and recomputes the rest, but here the peak moved to the end of the backward pass.
card.measured: Memory above inference, 16 hidden layers of 1,024, batch 2,048: backprop 246.4 MiB, checkpointing 198.4 MiB; one layer's kept input is 8 MiB (module 30, section 1).

objects.checked: README intro and §1: kept activations, gradients, Adam buffers; memory table (246.4, 198.4), '8 MiB' per layer, checkpointing bullet.

objects.idea: Nudge every weight along one random direction, both ways; the difference of the two losses gives the slope along it, with no memory beyond inference.
objects.image: A blindfolded walker taps the floor one step left and one step right, and leans toward the lower tap.

card.title: Two forward passes, one slope
card.text: MeZO draws a random direction z from a seed and measures the loss a small step ε along z each way. The difference is the slope along z, and the weights step along z. z is redrawn from its seed when needed, so nothing extra is stored. Most of each step is noise: from scratch it climbed to about 70%, then diverged in every seed; at half the rate it held, and reached about 75% in 40 epochs.
card.formula: g = (L(θ + εz) − L(θ − εz)) / 2ε;  θ ← θ − lr·g·z
card.measured: 0.0 MiB above inference at every depth, against 246.4 MiB for backprop at 16 hidden layers. On SST-2, 75.7% after 2,000 steps against LoRA's 91.5% after 300 (SmolLM2-360M-Instruct, module 30).

objects.idea: Forward-forward and Mono-Forward give each layer a goal of its own, so no error travels back through the stack.
objects.image: Each landing of the stair has its own small target pinned to its wall and its own dart; nobody shouts down from the top.

card.title: A goal for every layer
card.text: Forward-forward asks each layer for high 'goodness', the mean square of its outputs, on an image with its right label written in, and low on the same image with a wrong label. Mono-Forward gives each layer its own 10-way head and cross-entropy. Each still takes a gradient, but inside one layer. Mono-Forward came within 0.7 points of backprop and was the fastest.
card.measured: Test accuracy after 20 epochs, 3 seeds: backprop 88.9%, Mono-Forward 88.2%, forward-forward 84.6%; seconds per epoch 1.13, 0.77, 1.08 (FashionMNIST, module 30, section 2).

objects.idea: Predictive coding sends the error down one layer per settling step, by local moves, and it arrives about ten times smaller at each layer down.
objects.image: A whisper passed down a line of people, one ear per beat, quieter at every ear.

card.title: An error that fades
card.text: Each layer keeps a value that may differ from what the layer below predicts. Clamp the label on top, and each settling step moves the values to lower the energy, so the error reaches one more layer down per step. It arrives pointing the right way but scaled by γ^k, k layers below the top; in an 8-hidden-layer network, float32 rounding drowns it at the bottom two. It also held about twice backprop's memory.
card.formula: F = Σ ½‖x_l − μ_l‖² + cross-entropy at the top
card.measured: 8 hidden layers, on arrival: cosine 1.00 with backprop's gradient for the top six matrices and size 0.1^k (γ = 0.1); 502.5 MiB above inference at 16 layers against backprop's 246.4 (module 30, sections 1 and 3).

also.idea: Read a memory claim with its meter, and split the memory a rule saves from the memory its optimiser costs.
also.image: Two gauges by the door, one for tensors alive, one for the whole process; next to them, Adam's two buffers sit on the scale beside each weight.

card.text: At 16 hidden layers, Adam's two buffers per weight are half of backprop's extra memory: 246.4 MiB with Adam, 120.0 with plain SGD. Mono-Forward with SGD stays flat, 21.3 to 22.7 MiB from 2 to 16 layers, but with Adam it needs 150.2. The process meter reads up to 80 MiB more than the live-tensor meter, and ranks the rules in nearly the same order.

objects.idea: A model reads numbers, so text must first become symbols with ids; start from single bytes or characters.
objects.image: At the gate a sentence is pulled apart into loose letters that rattle into a tray, sixteen of them for 'low lower lowest'.

card.title: Start from single bytes
card.text: A model reads numbers, not text, so the text must first be cut into pieces with ids. The smallest pieces are bytes: 256 of them spell any text, so nothing is ever unknown, but sequences get long. Whole words make short sequences but need a huge vocabulary and still miss names and typos. Subwords sit between the two.

objects.checked: README 'Why subwords?' (256 bytes, long sequences, whole words and <unk>, subwords between); 'low lower lowest' is 16 characters counting the two spaces (formations.js TS).

objects.idea: Byte-pair encoding (BPE) counts every pair of neighbouring symbols, merges the commonest into one new symbol, and repeats.
objects.image: A gatekeeper glues the two letters he sees side by side most often into one tile, then counts again.

card.title: Merge the commonest pair
card.text: Byte-pair encoding (BPE) counts every pair of neighbouring symbols and merges the commonest pair into one new symbol. Then it counts again and repeats. When two pairs tie, the module's trainer takes the smallest pair, so the result is the same on every run. In 'low lower lowest', 'l'+'o' and 'o'+'w' each occur three times; the tie goes to the smallest pair, so 'l'+'o' merges first.

objects.checked: README 'Why subwords?' (merge the most frequent adjacent pair), 'The Zig lane' (tie-break: highest count, then lexicographically smallest pair); python/src/bpe.py best_pair; ran bpe.get_stats/best_pair on 'low lower lowest': first merge (108,111) = 'lo', count 3.

objects.idea: The ordered list of merges is the whole tokenizer: common words end as one token, rare words as a few pieces.
objects.image: The gatekeeper's ledger of glued pairs, in order, is all he needs to chop any new text that reaches the gate.

card.title: The merge list is the model
card.text: Training writes down each merge in order, and that list is the whole tokenizer. To encode new text, apply the merges in the same order. Common words end as one token, rare words as a few pieces. Production tokenizers first split text into words, numbers and punctuation, so merges never cross a word's edge; the module's own trainer skips that step, so its merges do cross spaces.

objects.idea: Byte-level BPE gives back exactly what it took: decoding the tokens of a text returns the same text, byte for byte.
objects.image: Tiles run through the gate and back out, and the sentence that leaves is letter for letter the one that came in.

card.title: Out exactly as it came in
card.text: Byte-level BPE starts from the 256 byte values, so it can write any string in any language. Encoding applies the learned merges; decoding joins the pieces back into the same bytes. So decode(encode(text)) equals text. The module tests that round trip in Python, and checks that its Zig trainer learns the identical list of merges.

also.idea: Tokenizers are unfair across languages: the same message costs more tokens in some languages than in others.
also.image: A toll booth that takes one coin a word from some travellers and two from others, for the same message.

card.title: Some languages pay more
card.text: Fertility is the number of tokens a tokenizer spends per word. English is cheap; French, Spanish and code cost more, so the same message uses more tokens, more compute and more of the context window. Tokens per word is rough, since languages use different numbers of words, so the module also compares whole sentences with their translations.

objects.idea: Attention is a soft dictionary lookup: each token's query is scored against every key, and the answer is the values averaged by those scores.
objects.image: A guest shines a torch around the atrium; the mirrors that face it flash brightest, and the guest pours together a cup from each holder, most from the brightest.

card.title: A soft dictionary lookup
card.text: A dictionary lookup is hard: one key matches and you get its value. Attention is the soft version. Three learned matrices turn each token into a query, a key and a value. Each query is scored against every key by a dot product, divided by √d_head so the scores do not grow with size and push the softmax to all or nothing. The softmax weights, which sum to 1, average the values.
card.formula: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q·Kᵀ / √d_head)·V

objects.idea: The causal mask: each token reads only itself and the tokens before it, in training as in generation.
objects.image: Every seat in the atrium has blinkers, so no guest can see anyone who came in later.

card.title: No peeking ahead
card.text: A model that learns to predict the next token must not see it. Set every score above the diagonal to minus infinity and the softmax gives it zero weight, so token t reads only tokens 0 to t. Train without the mask and the output comes to depend on later tokens, which do not exist when the model generates. Here the future did not even help: this small model scored worse with it in view.

objects.idea: Multi-head attention runs several small attentions side by side, and each head learns its own habit, such as reading the previous token.
objects.image: Each guest carries several torches with coloured lenses; one always points one seat back, another at the start of the line.

card.title: Each head learns a habit
card.text: Multi-head attention runs several attentions in parallel, each on a slice of the vector, then joins their outputs and projects them back. Each head is free to learn its own pattern. In the module's trained tiny GPT, some heads attend to the previous token, some to the start of the line, and some spread over recent context.
card.measured: Tiny GPT: 3 layers × 4 heads, d_model 128 (module 04, Step 2).

objects.idea: A block normalizes, attends and adds the result to the residual stream, then normalizes, runs a small network and adds again; repeat the block.
objects.image: The atrium repeats along the corridor like locks on a canal; at each, the guests and then a clerk tip a cupful into the blue channel, and it flows on.

card.title: Repeat the block
card.text: A block normalizes its input, applies attention and adds the result back; then it normalizes again, applies a small two-layer network and adds again. The running sum that every block reads from and adds to is the residual stream; the norm sits off that path, so the stream itself is never normalized. Token and position embeddings go in at the bottom; a score for every possible next token comes out at the top.

also.idea: Each token sends out a query and each token offers a key; the better a key lines up with the query, the larger its weight.
also.image: Each guest shines a torch; the others hold up mirrors, and the mirrors that face the torch flash brightest.

card.title: Query meets key
card.text: Each token emits a query, and every token, itself included, emits a key. The match score is their dot product: the better the key lines up with the query, the larger its weight after the softmax.

objects.idea: A convolution slides one small grid of weights over the image and writes a weighted sum at each place: it looks locally and shares its weights.
objects.image: A stamp the size of a postage stamp walks across a mural, inking one weighted sum at each spot onto a second wall.

card.title: One stamp, every place
card.text: A convolution slides a small grid of weights, the kernel, over the image and writes one weighted sum at each position. Each output sees only a small patch (locality), and the same weights are used everywhere (weight sharing), so shifting the image shifts the output the same way. Different weights pick out vertical edges, horizontal edges, blur or sharpening. That built-in bias is why CNNs learn from modest data.

objects.idea: Train a small CNN and its first-layer kernels turn, with no one asking, into oriented edge and blob detectors.
objects.image: The eight stamps on the door's shelf start as smudges and, as you watch, sharpen into edges at several angles and small dots no one carved.

card.title: Detectors nobody drew
card.text: Train a two-layer CNN to classify clothing images and look at its eight first-layer 5 × 5 kernels. They start as noise and end as oriented edge and blob detectors, like the kernels people once designed by hand. Nothing in the loss asks for edges; they are what helps.
card.measured: TinyCNN, 6 epochs on 6,000 FashionMNIST images: 79.3% on 1,000 held-out images (results/cnn.json).

objects.idea: A Vision Transformer cuts the image into patches, turns each into a token, and runs the same block as for text, without the causal mask.
objects.image: The picture is cut into square tiles, and the tiles walk in single file through the door into the atrium, where no one wears blinkers.

card.title: Pictures become tokens too
card.text: A Vision Transformer (ViT) cuts a 224 × 224 image into a 14 × 14 grid of 16 × 16 patches. Each patch is flattened and multiplied by a learned matrix to make a token, a position embedding is added, and one extra [CLS] token joins them. The same block as for text then runs with no mask, so every patch sees every patch. The [CLS] token's final state feeds the class head.
card.measured: ViT-tiny fine-tuned on bean-leaf diseases, 4 epochs: 95.3% on the test set (122 of 128) (results/finetune.json).

objects.checked: README intro, 'Theory bridge' diagram, 'What you'll see' 2 and the text/ViT table (196 patches + 1 [CLS], linear projection, no mask, [CLS] → class head), section 4; results/finetune.json (0.9531, 122/128).

objects.idea: CLIP scores a picture against written prompts and picks the best match, with no task training; on a narrow task, a short fine-tune still wins.
objects.image: Captions hang on hooks by the door; each picture walks to the caption nearest in meaning, and on the bean leaves it often walks to the wrong one.

card.title: Pictures meet captions
card.text: CLIP was pretrained to match images with captions. To classify with no training, write one prompt per class and pick the prompt that best matches the image. It can score any class you can write down, but on a narrow, specialist task it falls far behind a model fine-tuned for a minute. Scale and fine-tuning work together; one does not replace the other.
card.measured: Bean test set, prompts describing the symptoms: CLIP 43.8% (56 of 128), against 33% chance and 95.3% for the fine-tuned ViT-tiny (results/clip_zeroshot.json, results/finetune.json).

also.idea: Attention maps show where a ViT looks: the last layer's [CLS] attention, or attention rollout through every layer.
also.image: A lantern behind the picture lights up the tiles the guests are staring at.

card.title: Where the model looks
card.text: The [CLS] token's attention in the last layer shows which patches it reads most; the map is spiky. Attention rollout multiplies the attention of all 12 layers, each mixed half and half with the identity to stand in for the skip path, and gives a cleaner map. These show where information flows, not what the model uses: ViT-base calls a bean leaf a 'leaf beetle' yet still attends to the leaf.

objects.idea: A chat template wraps each turn in the special tokens the model was trained on; it may also add text you never wrote.
objects.image: Each speaker's words go in an envelope with an orange seal at each end; the model only learned to read sealed letters, and a clerk slips in a note of his own.

card.title: The envelope around each turn
card.text: An instruct model was trained on conversations in one exact format. Special tokens such as <|im_start|> and <|im_end|> mark where each turn starts and ends; the role names system, user and assistant are ordinary tokens. The chat template writes your messages into that format. It can add text you never wrote: SmolLM2's inserts a system turn when you send none, so print the template before you trust a prompt.

objects.idea: A learned table turns each token into a point; tokens used alike sit close, so July lands beside June and August before any layer runs.
objects.image: On the gallery floor, word-tiles gather into groups: months together, numbers together, countries together, code together.

card.title: Near means alike
card.text: The embedding table gives each token a vector, one row per token, learned with the rest of the model. Tokens used in the same contexts must lead to similar predictions, so training pulls their vectors together. Projected to 2D, numbers, months, countries, code keywords and colours form separate groups before any layer runs.
card.measured: Nearest tokens to 'July' in SmolLM2-360M-Instruct's table: 'June', then 'July' without its leading space, then 'August' and 'September' (module 05).

objects.checked: README 'Meaning is geometry' (PCA families: numbers, months, countries, code keywords, colors; July's neighbours); python/src/embeddings.py family lists; anatomy.json embeddings 47,185,920 = 49,152 × 960.

objects.idea: The model ends with one score for every token it knows; a softmax turns the scores into odds that sum to one.
objects.image: From the balcony a row of flags rises over the garden, one per token, each as tall as its odds; ' Paris' towers over the rest.

card.title: Guess the next token
card.text: One forward pass ends with one score, a logit, for every token in the vocabulary. Softmax raises e to each score and divides by the total, so the results are positive and sum to 1. Generation picks a token from these odds, appends it, and runs again.
card.formula: pᵢ = e^zᵢ / Σⱼ e^zⱼ
card.measured: After 'The capital of France is', 91% on ' Paris', 3.3% on ' located', out of 49,152 tokens: SmolLM2-360M-Instruct (results/sampling.json).

objects.checked: README intro (960-dimensional vector to next-token choice), 'A confident next token' (49,152 tokens, 91%); results/sampling.json top5 (0.9113, 0.0334).

objects.idea: Temperature, top-k, top-p and min-p reshape the odds before you draw a token; the model itself does not change.
objects.image: A wind on the balcony: cold, and only the tallest flag stands; warm, and the flags draw level; a gardener cuts the short ones before the draw.

card.title: Reshape the odds, then draw
card.text: Divide the logits by a temperature T before the softmax: T below 1 sharpens the odds toward the top token, T above 1 flattens them. Top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens. Top-p keeps the fewest tokens whose odds add up to p, so it keeps more when the model is unsure. Min-p keeps every token with at least a set fraction of the top token's odds.
card.formula: pᵢ ∝ e^(zᵢ/T)
card.measured: After 'My favorite color is': top-k 5 keeps 5 tokens, top-p 0.8 keeps 14; ' blue' holds 40%, so min-p 0.1 sets the bar at 4% and 5 tokens pass (results/sampling.json).

objects.checked: README 'Temperature reshapes the same logits', 'top-k is a count; top-p is a budget; min-p is a ratio'; results/sampling.json (kept top_k 5, top_p 14, min_p 5; blue 0.3981).

also.idea: Walk a real model's modules and add up its parameters by role: most sit in the MLPs, fewer in attention, some in the embedding table.
also.image: Thirty-two atria in a row; in each the torch-bearers fill one bench and the clerks of the small network fill three.

card.title: Where the weights live
card.text: Load the model, walk its modules, and add up the tensors by role. The layout is module 04's block repeated: norm, attention, add, norm, MLP, add. About two thirds of the parameters sit in the MLPs, about a fifth in attention, and an eighth in the embedding table, which the output head shares; the norms are almost nothing.
card.measured: SmolLM2-360M, 361.8M parameters in 32 layers: MLP 65.2%, attention 21.7%, embedding table 13.0% (results/anatomy.json).

also.idea: The logit lens reads each layer's hidden state through the final norm and output head; the layer where the final answer takes first place and keeps it is the decision layer.
also.image: Windows along the gallery each show a flag; from one window on, they all show the same winner.

card.title: Read every layer's guess
card.text: The logit lens takes the hidden state after each layer and pushes it through the final norm and output head, as if the model stopped there. Early layers give junk; at the decision layer the final answer reaches first place and stays. The lens reads early layers in the last layer's terms, which they do not use, so the junk means little.
card.measured: 'The Eiffel Tower is located in the city of': ' Paris' reaches rank 1 at layer 27 of 32 (71%) and ends at 98.5% (results/logit_lens.json).

objects.idea: Load a transformer from raw bytes: a manifest gives each tensor's name, shape and byte offset in one flat file of floats.
objects.image: A scribe unrolls one long scroll of numbers and snips it into labelled pieces.

card.title: One long scroll of numbers
card.text: The model file is one flat run of float32 numbers with no header. A separate manifest lists each tensor's name, shape, byte offset and count, in a fixed order. Loading means reading the manifest and pointing at the right bytes. The module's Zig engine loads module 04's GPT this way, with no framework.
card.measured: 619,776 parameters, 2.48 MB as float32: module 04's char-level GPT, loaded by module 07's Zig engine.

objects.idea: The KV cache keeps each token's key and value, so each new token costs one new row instead of a rerun of the whole text.
objects.image: Shelves along the scriptorium wall where each written token leaves its key and value, never written twice.

card.title: Keep what you computed
card.text: To write token 100, attention needs the keys and values of tokens 0 to 99. Without a cache the model reruns them all at each step, so a whole generation costs about n²/2 token passes. With the cache each step adds one row and reads the rest. The price is memory that grows with every token.
card.measured: 490 tokens per second with the cache against 8 without at 128 tokens of context (63×); 8× at 16 tokens, 30× at 64: Apple M5, one thread, module 07.

objects.checked: README 'The KV cache lab' table (582/72, 507/17, 490/8), n²/2 cost paragraph, 98,304 floats; Moves a39 numbers match

objects.idea: Prefill runs the prompt through to fill the cache; decode then adds one token at a time, and its new row has nothing for the causal mask to hide.
objects.image: The scribe first copies the page he was given, to stock his shelves, then writes on one letter at a time.

card.title: Prefill, then decode
card.text: Prefill pushes the prompt through the model to fill the cache. The module's Zig engine steps the prompt one token at a time; its self-check also runs the whole prompt in one pass under a triangular mask, and both give the same logits. Decode then adds one token per pass. The new token comes last, so every earlier position is allowed: the mask has nothing to hide in its row.
card.measured: Cached decode against a full masked pass: max |Δ| = 0; reading the cache one slot back gives max |Δ| ≈ 7, so the check catches cache bugs (module 07).

objects.checked: README Goals (prefill vs decode, mask vanishes), decode-loop flowchart (PREFILL: step each prompt token), KV cache lab (forwardFull, T×T masked score matrix, max |Δ| = 0, ≈ 7); figures/results.json selfcheck

objects.idea: Quantise the weights to int8: a quarter of the file size for almost no loss of quality; GGUF's Q8_0 does the same in blocks, Q4_K harsher.
objects.image: Pens that write with only 255 shades of ink, and a ledger of what was lost.

card.title: Fewer shades of ink
card.text: The module stores each weight as one of 255 levels, −127 to 127, with one float scale per row. GGUF's Q8_0 does the same in blocks of 32 weights with one fp16 scale each; Q4_K uses about 4.5 bits a weight. The engine turns int8 back into float32 when it loads, so decode is no faster here; on large models, reading fewer bytes per token is what makes real engines faster.
card.measured: 2.48 MB → 0.63 MB (3.9× smaller); held-out perplexity 4.6574 → 4.6568; largest logit change 0.06 (module 07).

objects.checked: README 'The quantization lab' (per-row symmetric, [-127,127], table, honest note on speed, GGUF Q8_0 blocks of 32 fp16 scale, Q4_K super-blocks of 256, ~4.5 bits); figures/results.json bytes and perplexities

also.idea: Sample by hand: temperature, then top-k, then top-p.
also.image: A bag of letter tiles in proportion to the odds; the scribe trims the bag before drawing.

card.title: Trim the bag, then draw
card.text: Sampling turns the model's scores into one token. Temperature divides the scores before the softmax: below 1 it sharpens the odds, above 1 it flattens them. Top-k keeps the k likeliest tokens; top-p keeps the smallest set whose odds reach p. Renormalise what is left, then draw.

also.checked: README Goals and exercise B (top-p: smallest set reaching p, then renormalise); zig/src/sampler.zig (temperature scaling, then top-k, then top-p)

also.idea: A parity test: the hand-written engine must give PyTorch's logits to within a tolerance.
also.image: Two scribes write the same page; laid one on the other, every letter lines up.

card.title: Two scribes, one page
card.text: A hand-written engine is right only if it matches a trusted reference. Feed the same prompt to both, compare the logits value by value, and fail if any differ by more than the tolerance. The Zig engine matches PyTorch to a largest gap of about 3 × 10⁻⁶, against a tolerance of 10⁻³.

also.checked: README intro (~3e-6), 'What you'll see' parity paragraph (tolerance 1e-3), Hands-on parity.py

objects.idea: A recurrent model carries one fixed-size state from token to token instead of keeping every past token.
objects.image: Next door the shelves grow; here a single satchel of fixed size is all anyone carries.

card.title: Memory need not grow
card.text: A GPT keeps a key and a value for every past token, so its memory grows with the text and each new token reads all of it. A recurrent model keeps one state of fixed size and updates it at each token. Its memory and its time per token stay flat however long the text.
card.measured: After 4,096 tokens: GPT cache 12,582,912 B, selective SSM state 106,400 B, GRU state 1,792 B. On the CPU the GPT slowed from 4,525 to 1,707 tokens per second; the SSM stayed near 4,600 (module 18).

objects.checked: README §3 'What each model keeps between tokens' (both tables), intro; Moves a66 numbers (12,582,912; 106,400; 1.575 vs 1.629) match §3

objects.idea: A GRU's update gate z decides, per unit and per token, how much of the old state to keep and how much to take from a new candidate.
objects.image: A satchel with a flap that opens a little or a lot, mixing old contents with the new.

card.title: A gate on the satchel
card.text: A GRU keeps one state vector h. At each token it proposes a candidate n and computes an update gate z between 0 and 1 for each unit. The new state keeps z of the old and takes 1 − z of the candidate. Near 1 a unit holds what it had; near 0 it rewrites.
card.measured: Two GRU layers of width 224: 619,808 parameters, 448 floats kept between tokens, validation loss 1.833 after 1,000 steps (module 18).

objects.checked: README §1 GRU equations (h ← (1 − z) ⊙ n + z ⊙ h; 'when z is near 1 … keeps its value'), parameter count, 2 × 224 = 448, table 1.833. P.gru checked: S[k+1] = lerp(S[k], C[k], 1 − Z[k]) = z·old + (1 − z)·candidate; caption 'keeps z = … of the old state' is right — the phase 1 inversion is fixed.

objects.idea: When the decay is fixed, a linear recurrence is a convolution: it trains in parallel and must match stepping one token at a time.
objects.image: A row of fading footprints that can be stamped all at once or one step at a time, with the same result.

card.title: A recurrence that is a convolution
card.text: If the state update is linear and its decay is the same at every step, the output is a fixed weighted sum of past inputs, with weights that fade with distance. That is a convolution, so training computes all positions at once. Generation runs the loop, one token at a time, and must give the same numbers.
card.formula: h_t = exp(Δ·A) ⊙ h_{t−1} + Δ·B·x_t
card.measured: The one-token loop matched the parallel form to 7.3 × 10⁻⁶ in the logits (module 18).

objects.checked: README §2 'Diagonal and fixed' (equation, kernel K[k] = Σ C·B·Δ·exp(k·Δ·A), parallel over 128 positions), 7.3 × 10⁻⁶; Goals; exercise (c)

objects.idea: A selective recurrence computes its decay from each token, so it chooses what to keep; no single kernel fits any more, and the convolution is gone.
objects.image: Each new footprint now decides how fast the old ones fade, so no single stamp fits the row and you must walk it step by step.

card.title: When the token decides
card.text: Mamba computes the step size, and so the decay, from each input: token by token, the layer chooses whether to write or to hold. The kernel then changes with the input, so the convolution trick is gone. Mamba-1 needs a custom parallel-scan kernel to train fast; the module uses Mamba-2's form, one decay per head and step, and trains it as one causal, decaying T × T matrix, while generation runs the loop.
card.measured: Selective model: validation loss 1.524 against the fixed one's 1.541 after 1,000 steps, one seed each; loop and matrix agree to 7.9 × 10⁻⁶ (module 18).

objects.checked: README §2 'Selective' paragraph (Δ, B, C from the input; convolution gone; Mamba-1 needs a parallel scan with a custom kernel; Mamba-2 form, 8 heads; T × T matrix), 7.9 × 10⁻⁶, table 1.541 / 1.524, 'one run of each'

also.idea: Count what each model keeps between tokens: the GPT's cache grows by 3,072 bytes a token, the recurrent states stay flat.
also.image: A rising pile of books next to a satchel that never gets heavier.

card.title: A pile against a satchel
card.text: The module steps each model through 4,096 tokens and counts the floats it holds after each one. The GPT adds 768 floats, 3,072 bytes, per token and passes the selective model's fixed 106,400 bytes after 35 tokens. GPT-2 small against Mamba-130M tells the same story: 70,778,880 against 2,949,120 bytes after 960 tokens.

also.checked: README §3 memory table and paragraph (768 floats, 3,072 B, 35 tokens); §4 table (GPT-2 / Mamba caches)

objects.idea: The state is a matrix S that stores values under keys: write v under k with an outer product, read with S k.
objects.image: A slate grid on the wall; touch a key at the head of a column and its value lights up down that column.

card.title: A matrix that answers
card.text: A linear-attention layer keeps its memory as a matrix S. To store a value v under a key k, add the outer product v kᵀ, scaled by a write strength β; to read, multiply S by a query. If the keys are orthogonal unit vectors and β = 1, S k returns exactly the value stored under k.
card.formula: write: S ← S + β v kᵀ   ·   read: S q

objects.checked: README intro ('write v under k; later S k returns it'), §1 state d_v × d_k, read S q, linear attention line with β

objects.idea: Linear attention only adds pairs to S; decay first shrinks S so old pairs fade; once S fills, every read blurs with the others.
objects.image: Chalk written over chalk until the slate is grey; a damp cloth fades the oldest writing.

card.title: Chalk over chalk
card.text: Linear attention only adds. Once there are more pairs than the key has dimensions, the keys cannot all be at right angles, so each read returns its value plus a little of every other. Decay multiplies S by α before each write, so old pairs fade and new ones read cleaner, at the price of forgetting. With α chosen per head and step from the input, decay is module 18's selective recurrence.
card.formula: S ← α S + β v kᵀ
card.measured: 64 random pairs in a 32 × 32 state: linear attention read 0.83 back right, about equally old and new; decay (α = 0.95) 0.40, keeping 0.98 of the newest 16 and 0.02 of the oldest (module 27).

objects.checked: README §1 four rules, decay = module 18's form (§2 check 1.4 × 10⁻¹³), capacity table (0.83, 0.40), by-age (0.83/0.82; 0.98/0.02)

objects.idea: The delta rule writes by correcting: read what S returns for k and write only the gap to v; that is one step of gradient descent.
objects.image: Before writing, the clerk reads what the slate says under that key and chalks in only what is missing or wrong.

card.title: Write by correcting
card.text: Before writing v under k, the delta rule reads what S already returns for k and writes only the difference. A key written twice then returns its new value, where linear attention returns a blend. The update is one step of gradient descent on ½‖S k − v‖², the error of the state's answer for k.
card.formula: S ← S + β (v − S k) kᵀ
card.measured: Overwrite test: delta rule's read has cosine 1.00 with the new value and −0.03 with the old; linear attention's 0.66 with each (module 27).

objects.checked: README §1 delta rule line, gradient-step derivation (autograd, gap 0 in float64), overwrite paragraph; Moves a67 (0.96/0.07 newest/oldest, 0.83 linear, 0.83 vs 0.47 over all 64) matches §1

objects.idea: The gated delta rule both decays and corrects; training computes it a chunk at a time, with one triangular solve per chunk.
objects.image: A clerk who chalks in only the difference and also wipes the whole slate a little before each write.

card.title: Correct, and wipe a little
card.text: The gated delta rule decays the whole state by α, then writes by correcting what the decayed state returns for k. Each correction depends on every earlier write, so token by token it is a slow loop. Within a chunk of 64 tokens the corrections form one lower-triangular system; one solve gives them all, and the chunk hands its last state to the next.
card.formula: S ← α S + β (v − α S k) kᵀ
card.measured: Chunks against the loop: largest gap 7.2 × 10⁻⁷; forward + backward 10 to 28 times faster on the Apple GPU, 7 to 13 times on the CPU (module 27).

objects.checked: README §1 gated delta line; §2 chunked form ((I + A) U = …, chunks of 64), gap table (7.2 × 10⁻⁷ gated delta), timing table and ratios. P.chunks code checked: decays S by α, then corrects against α S k — the gated delta rule.

also.idea: Fill one 32 × 32 state past its size: plain adding keeps a little of every pair; the rules that correct or fade keep the newest and lose the oldest.
also.image: One slate with more and more names chalked on; four clerks read them back, and the ones who rub out as they write lose the oldest names first.

card.title: How many names a slate holds
card.text: Write n pairs of random unit vectors into a 32 × 32 state and read every key back; a read is right when it lies closer to its own value than to any other. At 8 pairs every rule reads nearly all back. By 32 plain adding still does (0.99); delta has slipped to 0.81, decay to 0.75, gated delta to 0.56. Trained on a recall task, the size of the state mattered far more than the rule.

objects.idea: The forward process adds Gaussian noise on a fixed schedule, and a closed form jumps straight to any step.
objects.image: A fog machine in the corner turns a spiral of lanterns into haze, one puff at a time.

card.title: Add noise, a little at a time
card.text: Each step adds a little Gaussian noise on a fixed schedule. A sum of Gaussian draws is Gaussian, so any step can be reached in one jump. ᾱ_t, the share of the signal's variance left at step t, falls from 1 to near 0. Nothing here is learned.
card.measured: With T = 300 the usual linear schedule leaves √ᾱ_T = 0.22; scaled by 1000/T it leaves 0.006 (module 09).

objects.checked: README 'The forward process (fixed)' (closed form, ᾱ_t definition, 0.22 and scaling), Hands-on 2 (√ᾱ_T = 0.006); Moves a43 matches

objects.idea: Train a network to predict the noise that was added; one squared error is the whole loss.
objects.image: A guide in the fog points at each lantern and says how far the fog has pushed it.

card.title: Learn to name the noise
card.text: Pick a clean sample, a random step t and a random noise ε, and make the noisy sample in one jump. The network sees the noisy sample and t, and must output ε. The loss is the squared error between the two. The same loss trains a small MLP on 2-D points and a UNet on images.
card.formula: L = ‖ε − ε_θ(x_t, t)‖²
card.measured: Loss 0.2678 → 0.0480 over 40 epochs in 3.1 minutes: 376,833-parameter UNet, 10,000 FashionMNIST images, T = 300 (module 09).

objects.checked: README 'The reverse process (learned)' (loss, recipe, same objective for MLP and UNet), Hands-on 2 log; Moves a44 matches

objects.idea: Run it backwards: start from pure noise and remove the predicted noise, step by step, until data appears.
objects.image: The fog machine runs backwards, drawing the haze in puff by puff, until the spiral of lanterns stands clear.

card.title: Then run it backwards
card.text: Sampling starts from pure noise at t = T and walks down to 0. At each step the network predicts the noise and the sampler removes part of it; DDPM then adds a little fresh noise back. DDIM adds none and takes larger steps, so the same trained network needs far fewer steps; in diffusers that is a change of scheduler, not of model.

card.title: A whispered word steers
card.text: Stable Diffusion denoises a 64 × 64 × 4 latent from an autoencoder, not a 512 × 512 × 3 image. A CLIP text encoder turns the prompt into embeddings, which the UNet reads through cross-attention. Classifier-free guidance runs the denoiser with and without the prompt and extrapolates; a larger w follows the prompt more closely and gives less varied samples.
card.formula: ε = ε_uncond + w · (ε_cond − ε_uncond)

card.title: Fewer, longer strides
card.text: DDPM removes noise in many small random steps. DDIM uses the same trained network but takes larger, deterministic steps. In diffusers this is a change of scheduler, not a new model. Ten DDIM steps took 0.65 s and already gave a plausible image; 200 took 7.53 s and bought sharpness.

objects.idea: Flow matching trains a network on the straight-line velocity from noise to data; a single sampling step lands every point on the data's mean.
objects.image: Strings stretched straight from each noise point to a spiral point; cut to a single step, every point lands in the middle.

card.title: Straight strings, one step
card.text: Flow matching joins each noise point to a data point by a straight line and trains a network on the line's direction. Sampling follows the learned velocity from noise to data in Euler steps. At the start the best velocity is the data's mean minus the noise point, so one step sends every point to the mean. The learned paths still bend, since the network averages all lines through a point.
card.formula: x_t = (1 − t) x₀ + t x₁   ·   target: x₁ − x₀
card.measured: One step: spread 0.13 against the data's 1. Four steps reach a distance of 0.127 to the spiral; DDIM is still at 0.158 after 200 (module 33).

objects.idea: A masked diffusion model drops the causal mask, hides a random share of characters, and learns to guess them back.
objects.image: A line of blank tiles on a long table, filling in the surest letters first, in any order.

card.title: Guess the hidden letters
card.text: Take module 04's character model and drop its causal mask. In training, hide each character behind [MASK] with probability t and score the guesses on the hidden ones, weighted by 1/t. With that weight the loss is an upper bound on the true loss, in the same nats per character as a left-to-right model.
card.formula: loss = (1/t) × cross-entropy on the hidden characters, averaged per character
card.measured: At equal compute: left-to-right twin 1.748 nats per character, diffusion bound 2.562; six times the training brings it to 2.060 (module 33).

objects.idea: A masked model can fill a line in any number of steps; few steps fill many blanks blind to each other, and the reveal rule decides which go first.
objects.image: A dial on the table from 1 to 128; turned low, many letters appear at once and the line gets worse.

card.title: The step dial
card.text: Writing starts from 128 blanks and keeps 128 ÷ steps guesses per step. In one step every character is guessed alone, so the line is just character frequencies. More steps let each guess see the ones before it. Revealing the surest guesses first gives more real words, and more repeats.
card.measured: Six-times model, surest first: word score 0.13 at 1 step, 0.95 at 128, but only 10% of 4-grams distinct; at random: 0.42 at 128 (module 33).

objects.idea: Block diffusion writes left to right in blocks, unmasking inside each, and keeps finished blocks in a KV cache.
objects.image: The table is cut into short boards; each board fills by unmasking, then slides onto the scriptorium's shelf.

card.title: Board by board
card.text: Block diffusion writes a line in short blocks from left to right and unmasks inside each one. A finished block never changes, so its keys and values go into a cache, as in module 07, and later blocks read them without recomputing. Blocks of 1 give back a left-to-right model; one block of 128 is plain masked diffusion.
card.measured: The cache cut the positions run 4 to 13 times; blocks of 16 wrote 64 lines in 0.33 s against 1.10 s for plain masked diffusion, the same characters with or without the cache (module 33).

card.title: Who wins on repeated data
card.text: Train both on the same 100,000 characters, seen again and again. The left-to-right twin is best at epoch 64, then overfits; the diffusion model starts slowly and is still improving at 200, where its bound ends below the twin's loss. That crossover is not a win: the twin stopped at its best is 0.21 nats ahead, and 800 epochs did not close it. On the whole corpus the twin led throughout.

card.text: Module 04's character GPT at six widths, 4 layers each, trained on the same 4M characters at a constant learning rate. With no decay, the model after D tokens is what a run stopped at D would give, so one run gives the loss at every length. The three smallest end near a table of letter pairs (2.446 nats); the larger ones fall past it.
