objects.idea: A power law is a straight line on log axes: fit it by least squares, after checking the fitter on made-up data with a known exponent.
objects.image: A plumb line stretched across the footings, touching some water marks and missing others by a little.

card.title: A straight line on log axes
card.text: If L = c·N^(−α), then log L falls along a straight line in log N with slope −α. The fitter was first fed losses made from α = 0.1 with noise, and gave it back. On the real six points, the fit reads α = 0.074, but the points bend, and α ranged from 0.053 to 0.121 across token budgets, since no model had finished learning.
card.formula: log L = log c − α·log N
card.measured: α = 0.074, R² 0.962, six sizes at 4M tokens; fitter check: α = 0.1 given back as 0.1000 ± 0.0029 over 1,000 draws (module 19, section 2).

objects.checked: README §2: power-law definition, synthetic check (0.1003, mean 0.1000, SD 0.0029), α 0.074 R² 0.962, residuals, α by tokens table. Recomputed α = 0.0738 and residuals from results/fit.json.

objects.idea: Training costs about 6ND operations; at each budget the best size has the lowest loss, but runs that all stop at one length fake that optimum.
objects.image: A rope draped over the footings: at each budget its lowest point picks the size, and it steps up each time one footing ends.

card.title: Each budget, a best size?
card.text: N counts the parameters outside the token and position tables, about 12·layers·d². Training costs about 6ND operations: 2N per token forward, about 4N backward. Here, at every budget the winner was the smallest size whose run still reached it, so the frontier is a staircase that follows where the runs end. Finding a real best size needs runs long enough to pass it.
card.formula: C ≈ 6·N·D
card.measured: At all 40 budgets the winner was the smallest size whose run reached it; d 64 ended at 20.0 tokens per parameter (module 19, section 3).

objects.checked: README §1 (N definition, ~12·layers·d²); §3 (6ND split, 40 budgets, staircase, loss rises at hand-over 2.494 → 2.544, D/N 78.7 to 1.27, d 64 at 20.0, slope 0.76). 4,001,792 / 200,064 = 20.0.

card.title: Count before you build
card.text: N is every parameter except the token and position tables, about 12·layers·d²: 50,880 at d 32, 3,159,552 at d 256. Training costs about 6ND operations. 6ND leaves out attention scores, 24% of the forward pass at d 32 and 4% at d 256.

also.idea: Two large studies split compute differently: one put most of a larger budget into size, the other grew size and data together, about 20 tokens per parameter.
also.image: Two architects arguing over one plan, one adding floors, the other adding bricks to each floor.

card.title: Kaplan against Chinchilla
card.text: Kaplan et al. (2020) found the best size grows as C^0.73. Hoffmann et al. (2022, Chinchilla) found size and data both grow about as C^0.5, about 20 tokens per parameter. They traced much of the gap to the learning-rate schedule: Kaplan's checkpoints came from runs set for a longer length. This module's 0.76 is close to 0.73, but it measures a staircase, so read nothing into the match.

objects.idea: LoRA bets that the change fine-tuning makes to a weight matrix uses only a few directions, so it can be stored as two thin matrices.
objects.image: Lay the coat's alterations side by side and they all run along a few seams.

card.title: Most change lives in few directions
card.text: The rank of a matrix is the number of independent directions it uses; count its large singular values. LoRA bets the update ΔW has low rank for small changes of behaviour. In this module's trained update, 7 directions rebuild a slice of it, where the frozen weight it is added to needs 15. The bet fails for new skills: on code and maths, full fine-tuning learns updates of much higher rank, and LoRA falls behind.
card.measured: 48 × 48 slice of layer 0's q_proj: the rank-32 adapter's ΔW needs 7 directions for under 20% error, the frozen W₀ needs 15 (python/results/svd_explorable.json).

objects.checked: README 'Why LoRA works — low intrinsic rank', interactive blurb (7 vs 15); svd_explorable.py docstring (layer 0 q_proj, ex-a r=32 adapter, sliced 48×48); results/svd_explorable.json rank_for_20pct_error 7 and 15.

objects.idea: LoRA freezes each weight matrix and trains a detour of two thin matrices beside it: rank 16 trains 8.7M weights, 2.3% of the model.
objects.image: Two thin strips of cloth pinned beside the coat; the coat itself is never cut.

card.title: Two thin matrices beside a frozen one
card.text: LoRA keeps each attention and MLP weight W₀ frozen. A maps the input down to r numbers and B maps them back up; only A and B train, and their product is scaled by α/r. The adapter is small beside the model, 35 MB on disk at rank 16, and can be swapped in and out. Rank 4 and rank 32 reached the same held-out loss, though with α fixed the larger rank took smaller steps.
card.formula: W = W₀ + (α/r)·B·A
card.measured: Rank 16, α 32, every attention and MLP projection: 8.7M trainable of 362M, 2.3%. Held-out loss 0.6661 at rank 4, 0.6662 at rank 32.

objects.checked: README 'What you'll see', 'Why LoRA works', exercise (a); src/common.py LORA_R=16, LORA_ALPHA=32; results/heldout.json ex-a-r4/r32; formations.js F.lora caption '8.7M trainable, 2.3%, rank 16'.

objects.idea: LoRA's B starts at zero, so at step 0 the detour adds nothing and training starts from exactly the original model.
objects.image: The new strips start the same colour as the coat, so on day one nobody sees a change.

card.title: B starts at zero
card.text: A starts with small random values and B with zeros, so B·A is zero before the first step. The fine-tuned model therefore begins as the base model, and training moves it away from there. Module 17 uses the same fact: with the adapter at zero, the model and its reference are one and the same.

card.title: Read the loss with care
card.text: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) trains a trained model further, with the same next-token loss, on hand-picked conversations. This lab counted the loss on every token: the fixed system prompt, the chat markers and the users' turns as well as the replies. Held-out loss fell from 1.29 to 0.67, but on the replies alone only from 0.83 to 0.79. Many recipes mask the prompt so only the replies count.

objects.idea: Forgetting is the rise of a held-out loss on the old task while the model learns a new one, and it comes fast.
objects.image: Old books on a shelf whose ink fades as new books are pressed in beside them.

card.title: New learning can erase old
card.text: A small character model trained on Shakespeare then learns GSM8K's worked maths solutions. Forgetting is how much its held-out loss on Shakespeare rises. Full fine-tuning lost almost all it would lose in the first 25 steps. Asked to continue 'ROMEO:', it writes about pounds and costs.
card.measured: Full fine-tune: forgetting 1.238 nats per character after 600 steps, 1.229 by step 25; mean of 3 seeds (results/forget.json).

objects.idea: Replaying a little old data keeps most of the old skill at almost no cost to the new one.
objects.image: Every few new books, someone reads aloud from an old one and its ink darkens again.

card.title: Mix in a little of the old
card.text: Replay puts old examples in every batch: here 8 of each 32 windows were Shakespeare. It forgot a fifth as much as plain fine-tuning, for a new-text loss only 0.052 worse. Self-distillation toward the start model forgot more than replay. Part of LoRA's smaller forgetting was smaller learning: at the same new-text loss, a slower full fine-tune forgot less than either LoRA arm.
card.measured: Forgetting after 600 steps: full 1.238, replay 0.255, distill 0.481, lora4 0.724, lora32 0.921; replay's new-text loss 1.546 against full's 1.495.

objects.idea: A network that learns task after task can lose the ability to learn; continual backprop keeps it by swapping its least useful units for fresh ones.
objects.image: Shelves go dusty and stop taking books; a caretaker keeps swapping the least-used shelf for a new one.

card.title: Losing the ability to learn
card.text: Forgetting loses what you knew; loss of plasticity loses the means to learn. Over 800 shuffled-pixel FashionMNIST tasks, plain backprop with Adam did worse on each new task, while most of its units went dead. Continual backprop scores each hidden unit by its mean activation times its outgoing weights and now and then replaces the lowest-scoring one with fresh weights. That held accuracy within a point.
card.measured: Online accuracy, tasks 1–50 → 751–800: Adam 70.8% → 65.6%, continual backprop 71.2% → 70.3%; dead units at task 800: 62.7% and 23.5%; 3 seeds.

objects.checked: README section 4: setup, continual backprop rule, results table, bullets, P1–P5.

card.title: Compare at a matched score
card.text: Read every run at the same new-text loss, 1.940, the worst arm's end. There a full fine-tune at a ten times smaller rate forgot less than either LoRA arm. Replay forgot least of all.

also.idea: KL from the start model on the new task did not predict forgetting across methods; KL on the old text did, but it needs the old data.
also.image: A tape measure from each book's old spot to where it now stands: measured on the new shelf it misleads, on the old shelf it tells the truth.

card.title: Say where you measured
card.text: KL(start ‖ model) measures how far the next-character predictions moved from the start model's; it depends on which text you measure it on. On the new text it ranked six methods poorly: replay moved far there yet forgot least, and self-distillation moved least yet forgot more than replay. On the old text it ranked them almost perfectly, which is close to a tautology. On a real chat model's four LoRA runs, one with mild replay, KL on the new task did rank forgetting.
card.formula: KL(start ‖ model) = Σ p_start(c)·(log p_start(c) − log p_model(c))
card.measured: Spearman with forgetting, 18 final runs: KL on new text 0.35, on old text 0.998; SmolLM2-360M LoRA arms: 0.92 over 16 points.

objects.idea: Bradley-Terry: the chance one item beats another is a sigmoid of their score gap, so scores can be fitted from choices alone.
objects.image: A taster points at one of two glasses; the winner's score rises and the loser's falls, by more when the choice was a surprise.

card.title: Scores from choices
card.text: Give each item a hidden score s. A judge prefers i to j with probability σ(sᵢ − sⱼ), so only differences of scores matter. Fit the scores by making the observed choices likely; each choice pushes the winner up by one minus the chance it was given. With twelve made-up items, a few hundred choices recover the rough order; the exact order needs thousands, because two items sit only 0.075 apart.
card.formula: P(i beats j) = σ(sᵢ − sⱼ);  loss = −log σ(s_winner − s_loser)
card.measured: 12 items, mean Kendall τ over 20 judges: 0.545 at 30 choices, 0.894 at 300, 0.985 at 10,000 (results/bt_synthetic.json).

objects.checked: README section 1 (formula, gradient), 1a table and paragraph.

objects.idea: DPO turns Bradley-Terry into a loss on the model itself: widen the gap between chosen and rejected replies, each measured against a frozen reference.
objects.image: Two glasses on a balance, the pan tied by a short leash to the old balance.

card.title: DPO: the model is the judge
card.text: RLHF seeks high reward with a KL penalty that keeps the model near a frozen reference. Solving that objective writes the reward as β times the log-ratio of the model's and the reference's probability of a reply, plus a term that cancels in Bradley-Terry. So DPO needs no separate reward model and no sampling. Here both replies grew less likely; the rejected ones fell further, and the loss only asks that the gap grow.
card.formula: loss = −log σ(β·[(log π(y_w) − log π_ref(y_w)) − (log π(y_l) − log π_ref(y_l))])
card.measured: TRL + LoRA rank 16, 200 steps: implicit reward picks the chosen reply on 58.5% of 200 held-out pairs; log π fell 0.05 nats for chosen, 0.48 for rejected.

objects.checked: README section 2 derivation, section 3 setup, results table and paragraph; results/dpo_full.json via README.

objects.idea: A teacher's soft odds say more than a hard label; dividing logits by a temperature above 1 lets the small odds say more.
objects.image: The big press shows its faint second guesses too, not just the boldest letter.

card.title: Soft targets say more
card.text: A one-hot label marks the right answer and nothing else. The teacher's odds also say which wrong answers are nearly right. Dividing the logits by a temperature T above 1 flattens the odds, so the small ones carry more weight.
card.formula: p_T = softmax(z / T)
card.measured: After 'window b', module 04's char-GPT gives e 0.48, y 0.12, u 0.11.

objects.checked: README section 1 opening and formula; exercise (a); formations.js DTE values.

objects.idea: Distillation trains a small student to match a big teacher's whole set of odds, not only the right answer.
objects.image: A big press hands its print to a small press, which learns to copy it.

card.title: A big model teaches a small one
card.text: The loss mixes cross-entropy on the true next character with the KL divergence from the teacher's softened odds. The T² factor keeps the two gradients on the same scale. A student at 48% of the teacher's size ended lower when distilled than when trained from scratch, on all three paired seeds, yet both stayed far above the teacher.
card.formula: loss = (1 − α)·CE + α·T²·KL(teacher_T ‖ student_T), T = 2, α = 0.5
card.measured: Validation loss, mean of 3 seeds: distilled 2.029, from scratch 2.066, teacher 1.724; 1,000 steps.

objects.checked: README section 1 formula, T and α, teacher/student sizes, table, 'What this shows'.

objects.idea: Magnitude pruning zeroes the smallest weights first; a random cut of the same size, the control, breaks the model.
objects.image: Shears clip the thinnest twigs first; clip the same number at random and the tree dies.

card.title: Remove the smallest
card.text: In each of the 224 attention and MLP matrices, zero the same share of weights, smallest |w| first. At 10% the reply to a test prompt is unchanged word for word; a random 10% writes 'Up! Up! Up!'. At 50% even magnitude pruning writes noise. Zeroed weights save no bytes: the matrices keep their shape.
card.measured: Perplexity 16.07 untouched; 10% smallest 16.41, 10% random 714.8; 50% smallest 1,485.5.

objects.idea: Quantising stores each weight in fewer bits: int8 with one scale per row, or 4 bits with a scale and bias for every 64 weights; then count the bytes.
objects.image: The press squeezes a fat book into a thin one: 723.6 MB down to 203.6 MB.

card.title: Sixteen levels per weight
card.text: Four bits give each weight one of 16 levels. With one scale per row, one large weight stretches the levels and leaves few near zero, where most weights sit. A scale and a bias per group of 64 weights cost half a bit more per weight and fix most of it. This is fake quantisation: it measures the damage, not speed.
card.formula: q = round((w − b)/s) in 0..15;  w′ = q·s + b
card.measured: Perplexity / bytes: untouched 16.07 / 723.6 MB; int8 per row 16.12 / 362.5 MB; 4-bit per row 36.15 / 182.3 MB; 4-bit group 64 19.94 / 203.6 MB.

objects.checked: README section 3 rules, group explanation (4 + 32/64 = 4.5 bits), table, bullets (3.98 vs std 0.18), fake quantisation; formations.js F.quant q16 caption '16 levels'.

objects.idea: BitLinear trains with block weights in {−1, 0, 1}, 8-bit inputs and a straight-through gradient that updates hidden float weights.
objects.image: Every coin in the room is minus one, zero or one, and the shopkeeper learns to price with them.

card.title: Train with three values
card.text: Each linear layer in the blocks rounds its weights to −1, 0 or 1 times one scale per matrix, and its inputs to 8 bits, in every forward pass. Rounding has no useful slope, so the backward pass treats it as if it were not there and updates float latent weights, which only training keeps. That is why training matters: a trained float model rounded to ternary afterwards goes from 1.69 to 4.34 nats.
card.formula: g = mean|W|;  code = clamp(round(W/g), −1, 1);  W′ = code·g
card.measured: Exercise (a): module 04's char-GPT rounded to ternary after training, 1.69 → 4.34 nats per character.

objects.idea: Compare models at the same file size, not the same parameter count, and tune every arm's shape and rate before you judge.

card.title: Same file size, every arm tuned
card.text: Each arm got shapes whose file fit the same budget, and its rate tuned on a held-out half no reported score looked at. At 1.5 MB the ternary model won; at 0.5 MB it tied with 4-bit. The planned margin over 4-bit was mostly a badly tuned baseline: giving one shape its own rate took away 0.137 of 0.168. Shape and rate moved the loss more than the format did.

objects.idea: Rounding the KV cache to 8 or 4 bits costs little and 2 bits breaks; keys round better per channel, and a rotation spreads outlier channels.
objects.image: Through the north window, the scriptorium's shelves below are spun so the few tall books' height spreads along the whole shelf before the shelf is cut lower.

card.title: Round the cache too
card.text: SmolLM2-360M keeps a key and a value per layer and key head for every past token: 40,960 bytes per token in bf16. Rounded per token, a group is one token's 64 channels; per channel, it is 64 tokens of one channel. Keys carry a few large channels, so per channel rounds them better. A Hadamard rotation mixes all 64 channels without changing attention scores, which spreads a large channel; it helped per-token keys a lot at 2 bits but hurt per-channel ones.
card.measured: Perplexity at 2 bits: keys per channel 44.45, per token 562.46, per token rotated 65.07; untouched 16.08. 4-bit cache: 0.28 of the bf16 bytes.

objects.checked: README section 3 (bytes per token, layouts, rotation, table, bullets), section 4 table and bytes; P9–P15.

also.idea: Casting the hidden float weights to bf16 at export can push some just over the threshold back onto it, and change a ternary model's codes.
also.image: A coin passed through the mint's press comes out a slightly different coin.

card.title: The bf16 cast at export
card.text: bf16 keeps only 8 significant bits, so a latent just above the threshold 0.5·g can land exactly on it, and rounding sends an exact half to 0. After normal training the cast flipped 0.12 to 0.16% of codes and the loss did not move. After a fine-tune at a tiny rate it undid 39% of the code changes. The fix: write the codes from the fp32 latents.

also.checked: README section 2 (bf16, threshold, both tables, fix); P7, P8.

objects.idea: In-context learning: a model reads a few solved examples in its prompt and carries the pattern to a new case, with no weight changed.
objects.image: A clerk reads the solved slips pinned along the desk and fills in the blank one at the end the same way.

card.title: Learning inside the prompt
card.text: Show a trained model a few solved examples and then a new case; it answers the new case in the same way. Nothing in the model changes: the examples work only while they sit in the prompt. Each prompt in this module's regression task holds a fresh rule, so the net cannot have memorised it and must read it from the pairs.

objects.checked: README intro, section 1 (fresh w per prompt, causal mask), section 4 table (79.4%, 88.6%, 84.2% coin-flip), Goals.

objects.idea: On a line-fitting task, a trained transformer's guesses come close to least squares on the pairs in its prompt, far closer than one gradient step, but not exact.
objects.image: The clerk's pencil line lies almost on a ruler laid through the pins, and pulls closer as pins are added.

card.title: Close to a fit, not exact
card.text: A 2-block transformer was trained on prompts of (x, y) pairs, each with a fresh 5-dimensional linear rule, and asked to guess y for a new x. Its error falls with every few pairs added and beats one gradient step about five times over at 10 pairs. Least squares is exact from 5 pairs on; the net levels off near 0.03 and does not reach it within 20 pairs.
card.formula: error = MSE / d; guessing 0 scores 1
card.measured: MSE/d at 10 pairs: net 0.075, one gradient step 0.372, least squares 0.000; net 0.034 at 20 pairs. All three bars set before the run were missed (module 20, results/icl.json).

objects.idea: On a real model, score a few-shot prompt from the next-token scores of the two label words, and read every gain against its interval.
objects.image: Two lamps, 'positive' and 'negative', over the desk; with one example slip pinned up, the right lamp is brighter far more often, and more slips change little.

card.title: Two logits decide
card.text: SmolLM2-360M-Instruct reads a prompt of k solved reviews and a new one; we compare its next-token scores for ' positive' and ' negative' and take the larger. One example lifts accuracy by 9.3 points; four and eight add nothing the intervals can tell apart. With coin-flip labels on the same eight examples it still beats no examples by 4.8 points, though the intervals just touch, so part of the gain may be the format and the label words, not the task.

objects.idea: Chain of thought: let a model write its steps before the answer; on 200 school maths problems a small model went from 15% to 61.5%.
objects.image: On the slate wall one scribe writes a bare number and is mostly wrong; the next works the sum line by line and is right far more often.

card.title: Let it think out loud
card.text: Asked for the answer at once, a small model has nowhere to do its arithmetic. Asked to write its steps first, it works on the page. The steps cost tokens: about 14 times as many.
card.measured: 15.0% answer only (13 tokens a problem), 61.5% with written steps (189): Qwen3-1.7B at 4 bits, first 200 GSM8K test problems, greedy, module 22.

objects.idea: Self-consistency: sample several chains and keep the most common answer; the share of problems where any sample is right is the ceiling.
objects.image: Eight scribes work the same problem on eight slates; five reach the same number and it is circled, while the odd ones out each reach a different number.

card.title: Sample many, take the vote
card.text: Sample chains at a temperature above 0 and keep the answer most of them reach. Wrong chains tend to end at different numbers; right ones agree. A vote can only pick an answer some sample gave, so 'any of n right' is its ceiling.
card.measured: One sample 61.1%, vote of 8 69.5%, any of 8 right 80.0%, temperature 0.7: Qwen3-1.7B at 4 bits, 200 GSM8K problems, module 22.

objects.image: A coin box under each method; the first coins buy a big jump, and eight times more coins buy only a little more.

card.title: Pay in tokens
card.text: Put every method on one axis: tokens the model writes per problem. Writing steps costs about 14 times answer only and adds 46.5 points; the next eight times, from one chain to eight, adds about 8. Best-of-n, which grades each sample, also reads about 298 tokens more per sample; this count leaves that out.
card.measured: 13 tokens 15.0%; 189 tokens 61.5%; 1,517 tokens 69.5% (vote of 8): module 22.

card.title: A grader that always says yes
card.text: Ask the same model, in a fresh chat, whether a sample is correct, and read the log-odds of Yes against No instead of its reply. Its top token is Yes for 1,587 of 1,600 samples, so its verdict is useless. Its log-odds still put a random right sample above a random wrong one 82% of the time, and keeping the top-graded of 8 beat the plain vote by one point.
card.formula: log-odds = log P(Yes) − log P(No)
card.measured: Best-of-8 70.5% against vote of 8 69.5%; AUC 0.82; top token Yes for 1,587 of 1,600 (module 22).

objects.idea: Treat the instruction as the one parameter of a frozen model: another model proposes instructions, a fixed scorer rates each on 60 training questions, and the best is kept.
objects.image: A sign-painter paints sign after sign, tries each on sixty visitors, and hangs the best one.

card.title: Tune the prompt like a weight
card.text: The model is frozen; only its instruction moves. A program reads the model's next-token scores for six question types, so the same instruction always gets the same score. A second model proposes instructions, from examples (APE) or from its own score history (OPRO), under one budget of 2,400 scored questions.
card.measured: Test accuracy 49.0% for the baseline instruction; 59.3% to 63.1% on average for the four methods: Qwen3-1.7B at 4 bits, TREC question types, 3 seeds, module 34.

objects.checked: Intro, section 1 (scorer, splits, budget 2,400, baseline 49.0%), section 2 (APE, OPRO), section 5 table (59.3 to 63.1).

objects.idea: A GEPA-style loop reads a few answers with feedback, writes a child instruction, and keeps it only if it beats its parent on those questions.
objects.image: The painter reads six visitors' complaints, paints a new sign from an old good one, and hangs it only if those six prefer it.

card.title: Reflect, mutate, keep the winners
card.text: Each step draws a parent from the candidates that are best on at least one training question, shows the optimiser six of its answers marked right or wrong, and asks for a child. A child that gets more of the six right than its parent is scored on all 60 and joins the pool. Of the four methods it had the best train and held-out means.
card.measured: 222 children over 3 seeds, 96 (43%) won their six; held-out 69.3 ± 1.2%, test 62.3 ± 8.4% (module 34).

objects.checked: Section 4 loop steps and counts (222, 96, 43%), table (69.3 ± 1.2, 62.3 ± 8.4), section 5 table.

objects.idea: The best of many prompts on 60 questions is partly luck: only questions the search never saw tell how good it is.
objects.image: The winning sign is carried out to three hundred strangers and scores lower there than it did on the sixty.

card.title: Check on unseen questions
card.text: Choosing the best of 30 to 40 instructions on 60 questions picks partly for luck, so the winner's training score overstates. A held-out split from the same source shows by how much. A test set with another mix of question types can reorder the methods again.
card.measured: Chosen instructions scored 8.4 to 10.1 points higher on train than on held-out, against 4.7 for the baseline (module 34).

objects.checked: Section 5 'The overfitting gap' (8.4 to 10.1, 4.7, 30 to 40 candidates), 'Held-out and test tell different stories' (9% and 25% of descriptions).

also.idea: A text 'gradient' is a written critique of the errors, turned into an edit; unlike a gradient it has no size and no sure sign, so most edits made things worse.
also.image: A critic pins a note of complaints to the sign; the painter repaints to follow it, and scrapes the new paint off when the visitors like it less.

card.title: A gradient with no size
card.text: Show the optimiser the instruction and the questions it got wrong, ask what caused the errors, then ask for a rewrite. Keep the rewrite only if training accuracy does not fall. A real gradient step, small enough, always lowers the loss on its batch; these critiques lowered training accuracy in most steps, and cannot be scaled or added.
card.measured: Of 117 edit steps over 3 seeds, 12 raised training accuracy, 4 tied, 101 lowered it and were undone (module 34).

also.checked: Section 3 steps 1 to 4 and 'Most steps went the wrong way'; 'What is like gradient descent' point 2.

objects.idea: An embedding model turns a text into a unit vector so that close meanings lie close; search ranks texts by cosine. A language model's averaged states make a poor search key.
objects.image: Books gather into shelves by topic as a trained cataloguer files them; an untrained one leaves every book a little close to every other.

card.title: Search by angle
card.text: Run a text through a model, average the vectors of its real tokens, and scale to length 1; the cosine of two such vectors is their dot product. MiniLM, trained on pairs of related texts, keeps unrelated pairs near 0. SmolLM2, trained to predict the next token and then to chat, never to embed, makes every pair look fairly alike, so the right paragraph rarely wins among 2,067.
card.formula: v = mean of token states over real tokens; v = v / |v|; score = v_q · v_p
card.measured: Right paragraph ranked first: MiniLM 62.5%, SmolLM2 mean-pooled 10.6%; median cosine with a random paragraph 0.01 and 0.69 (module 21).

objects.checked: Section 1 code and table (median cosines 0.58/0.86 gold, 0.01/0.69 random), section 2 recall table (62.5%, 10.6%) and SmolLM2 paragraph.

objects.idea: BM25 scores a passage by the words it shares with the question: rare words count most, repeats count less and less, and long passages need more matches.
objects.image: A card catalogue with one drawer per word, listing the books that hold it; the drawers of rare words hold few cards, and each of those cards counts the most.

card.title: Count shared words, weigh rare ones
card.text: An inverted index lists, for each word, the paragraphs that hold it, so a query reads only its own words' lists. BM25 then adds up each shared word: its idf (rarity), damped for repeats by k1 and for long paragraphs by b. Plain word counting put the right paragraph first more often than MiniLM's vectors did.
card.measured: Recall@1 on 10,570 SQuAD questions: BM25 75.5%, MiniLM 62.5% (module 21).

objects.checked: Section 2 formula, k1 and b, inverted index table, recall table (75.5, 62.5).

objects.idea: Retrieval-augmented generation: paste the top passage into the prompt and let the model answer; giving it the right passage shows how much error is the reader's.
objects.image: The librarian hands a page to a reader at the desk; a referee checks whether a wrong answer came from the wrong page or from a bad reading of the right one.

card.title: Fetch, paste, answer
card.text: SmolLM2-360M-Instruct answered 200 SQuAD questions with no passage, with BM25's top paragraph, and with the paragraph the question was written on. The right paragraph is the ceiling: a perfect retriever would add 8 points of exact match over BM25, while the reader loses the other 63. A wrong passage helps about as little as none.
card.measured: Exact match: no passage 4.5%, BM25 top-1 29.0%, right paragraph 37.0%; with a wrong top-1 paragraph 4 to 6% (module 21).

objects.checked: Section 3 setup and table (4.5, 29.0, 26.0, 37.0; 5.9% and 4.2% when not gold), 'What the table shows' (8 points, 63 points).

also.idea: Measure a retriever by recall@k, the share of questions whose right paragraph comes back in the first k; here word matching beat a neural search.
also.image: Two librarians race to the right shelf; the one who reads the words on the spines gets there first more often.

card.title: Plain word counts held up
card.text: On SQuAD, BM25 put the right paragraph first for 75.5% of 10,570 questions, MiniLM for 62.5%. SQuAD's writers read the paragraph before writing each question, which may favour shared words; this run tests none of the reasons offered.

also.checked: Section 2 recall table and 'Reading it, hedged'.

also.idea: An agent can keep memory in four places: the prompt, a running summary, a retrieval store, or its weights, and each fails in its own way.
also.image: Four places to leave a note: on the desk in front of you, in a notebook you rewrite, in a filing cabinet, or carved into the desk itself.

card.title: Four places to remember
card.text: The prompt runs out of room and costs more as it grows. A running summary loses detail at each rewrite. A retrieval store can return the wrong passage, which the reader then trusts. Writing to the weights by fine-tuning is slow, cites no source, and makes one fact hard to remove.

also.checked: Section 4 text and table.

objects.idea: A model alone only turns text into text; an agent is a model, some tools and a loop that runs them.
objects.image: A voice at the bench can only speak; three hands on the wall, holding a calculator, a card index and a file list, wait for its word.

card.title: A model, tools and a loop
card.text: On its own a language model cannot look anything up or run anything: text goes in, text comes out. Let it write which tool to call and with what input; plain code parses that line, runs the tool, and pastes the result back into the prompt. Repeat until it gives a final answer or hits a step limit.

objects.checked: 'What is an agent?' (text -> text, LLM + tools + loop), section 1 (three tools, the 70-line loop, step limit in 'Looping').

objects.idea: The ReAct loop: the model writes a thought and an action, the tool's reply comes back as an observation, and 'Final Answer' ends the run.
objects.image: A ticker tape prints thought, action, observation, round and round, then prints the answer and the hands fall still.

card.title: Thought, action, observation
card.text: Each turn the model writes a Thought in words and an Action naming a tool and its input. The loop runs the tool and appends its output as an Observation. 'Final Answer' stops the loop, but it marks the end of a run, not a right result; only a separate check makes it a success.
card.measured: kb_lookup[seconds in a day] → 86400, calculator[86400 * 3] → 259200, Final Answer 259200: SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, temperature 0, module 10.

objects.checked: 'What is an agent?' (ReAct), section 1 condensed trace and transcripts/handrolled_trace.txt; exercise B (3.67 marked OK, transcripts/exercise_b_before_after.txt).

objects.idea: Code as action: the model writes a short program that calls the tools, so several calls and the arithmetic fit in one step.
objects.image: Instead of one shouted command, the voice hands the workshop a written recipe, and the hands work through it in one go.

card.title: Code as the action
card.text: smolagents' CodeAgent lets the model write Python that calls tools, does arithmetic and passes results along; a restricted interpreter runs it. The lookup and multiply that took the hand-written loop two turns took one step. The cost: you run code a model wrote, and the interpreter is not a full sandbox.
card.measured: seconds_in_day = kb_lookup("seconds in a day"); calculator(f"{seconds_in_day} * 3") → 259200 in one step; (2 ** 10 + sqrt(144)) * 3 − 100 → 3008: SmolLM2-1.7B, module 10.

objects.checked: 'Two ways to act', section 2 snippet and 3008, transcripts/smol_trace.txt.

also.idea: MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a standard way to offer tools and data to agents, so a tool written once works with any agent that speaks it.
also.image: One wall socket that every tool's plug fits.

card.title: One plug for many tools
card.text: This module wires its tools in by hand. MCP offers tools and data as a service that any agent or app speaking the protocol can find and use. Since December 2025 the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation runs it.

also.checked: 'Where to go next in the Agents & MCP courses'.

also.idea: Small models drift from the format, repeat a failed call, or act when told only to report; and text from a tool can carry orders, so check every step.
also.image: A hand reaches again and again for the same wrong drawer, and a note slipped in with a tool's result tries to give orders.

card.title: Where agents break
card.text: Format drift: the call lands inside the thought and the parser finds nothing; a one-shot example in the system prompt fixed it. Looping: the first lookup tool joined two suggested keys in one string, and the model sent it back four times; a recovery rule fixed it. Every observation goes back into the prompt, so a tool's text can carry orders; this module's agent has no defence.

also.checked: Section 1 'How a small model fails', kb_lookup_naive paragraph, transcripts/handrolled_trace.txt (four repeated calls), section 5 (prompt injection, CaMeL).

also.idea: An agent that samples is a random process: run each task many times and report the success rate, not one demo.
also.image: Ten benches run the same job side by side; a tally board shows how many finished right.

card.title: Report the bar, not the demo
card.text: At temperature 0.5 the same task can succeed or fail. A 1.7B model was perfect on a lookup then a multiply, yet rewrote a bracketed sum and did arithmetic on a number it was only asked to report. You learn a task is a 10% task only by running it ten times.
card.measured: Success over 10 runs at temperature 0.5: 100% look up seconds in an hour then ×2, 90% 2 ** 10, 80% capital of Japan, 20% (5 + 7) * 3, 10% report the speed of light: SmolLM2-1.7B, module 10.

objects.idea: A bandit gives no labels, only rewards: ε-greedy, UCB1 and Thompson sampling each trade trying levers against using the best, and regret counts the cost.
objects.image: A shed of five levers that pay at unknown rates; under each, a chalk tally of pulls and wins, the tally under the best lever growing fastest.

card.title: Explore, then exploit
card.text: Five levers pay 1 with their own unknown odds. Regret is the wins lost against a player who knew the best lever from the start. ε-greedy pulls a random lever 10% of the time forever, so its regret grows in a straight line. UCB1 adds a bonus to levers pulled rarely; Thompson sampling draws a guess of each lever's odds from its record and pulls the best guess.
card.formula: UCB1: argmax  mean + √(2 ln t / n)
card.measured: Median regret after 10,000 pulls, 20 seeds: Thompson 43, UCB1 228, ε-greedy 237, random 2,207.

objects.checked: README Goals; §1 Bandits (five arms 0.2–0.7, regret definition, rule definitions, results table, ε-greedy straight-line growth); results/bandits.json not needed beyond README table. formations.js F.bandit: BP=[.4,.2,.7,.5,.6] five arms, labels A–E, 'N pulls' caption: correct.

objects.idea: REINFORCE makes each action taken likelier in step with the return that followed it, the discounted sum of later rewards.
objects.image: A cart balancing a pole; after each run, the pushes that had a long run still ahead of them are chalked to be likelier next time.

card.title: Make good actions likelier
card.text: A small network gives the probability of pushing the cart left or right. REINFORCE plays one episode, then raises the log-probability of each push in proportion to the return that followed it. Subtracting the episode's mean return and dividing by its spread keeps the step size steady. Nothing stops one bad step from undoing a good policy.
card.formula: loss = −Σₜ log π(aₜ|sₜ) · (Gₜ − mean G) / std G
card.measured: All three seeds reached a 500-step episode within 13,684 steps; two ended holding the pole for all 500 steps, seed 0 for about 121.

objects.checked: README §3 REINFORCE (network 4→64→2, γ 0.99, loss, normalisation, seed table 9,781 / 7,804 / 13,684; greedy 121.2, 500, 500), CartPole env (two pushes of ±10 N). F.policy caption checked: wrong, see formation_issues.

objects.idea: PPO clips each update so the new policy stays near the old one; at the same high rate, clipped runs held the pole, unclipped runs rose and then collapsed.
objects.image: A governor on the cart's engine that stops any lurch; beside it, a cart without one that speeds up, then crashes.

card.title: But not too fast
card.text: PPO reuses each batch for several updates. It clips ρ, the ratio of the new to the old probability of an action, to [0.8, 1.2], so an update gains nothing by pushing further. A second network, the critic, judges each action by how much better it did than expected, the advantage A.
card.formula: L = mean(min(ρ·A, clip(ρ, 0.8, 1.2)·A))
card.measured: At rate 2.5 × 10⁻³, all three clipped seeds ended at 500; unclipped, they ended at 9.1, 190.1 and 108.9.

objects.checked: README §4 PPO (ratio, clip 0.2, critic, GAE, results table lr 2.5e-3 with and without clip). F.curves with CLIP spec: labels 'clipped', 'no clip', 'training →', 'reward'; see formation_issues.

also.idea: Q-learning learns the value of each move in each cell of a grid; check the learned values against breadth-first search.
also.image: A grid on the shed floor where numbers spread out from the goal tile, cell by cell.

card.title: Learn a value per cell
card.text: On a 10 × 10 grid with two walls, each move costs 1, so a cell's value under the best policy is minus its moves to the goal, which breadth-first search gives exactly. Q-learning nudges one table entry halfway to what it just saw after each move. Starting every entry at 0 makes untried moves look best, so the agent explores. After 300 episodes the greedy path took the shortest route, 36 moves, in 20 of 20 seeds.

also.checked: README §2 Tabular Q-learning (10 × 10, two walls with one gap each, reward −1, α 0.5, ε 0.1, Q = 0 start, shortest path 36, greedy 36 in 20 of 20 seeds).

objects.idea: A checker reward: sample a group of eight replies, mark each right or wrong with a program, and push up the replies that beat the group's mean.
objects.image: A teacher's hut where eight answers to one sum come in at once; the right ones are stamped and rise, the wrong ones sink.

card.title: Grade with a program
card.text: A small model adds 3-digit numbers, and a checker program reads its final number: 1 if right, else 0. For each sum the model samples a group of 8 replies. A reply's advantage is its reward minus the group's mean, so replies above the mean become likelier. A group where all 8 score the same teaches nothing. Most of the gain was a change of style: the model learned to write out its column sums, which it already did well.
card.formula: Aᵢ = rᵢ − mean r
card.measured: pass@1 59.1% → 94.9% after 300 steps with Dr. GRPO; worked-style replies 24.7% → over 98%.

objects.checked: README §1 (task, checker, base 59.1%, worked 24.7%, worked right 91.2%), §2 (G = 8, 32 sums, 300 steps, advantage table, all-equal group teaches nothing, results table), What the runs show. F.checker('grade'): 8 replies CR=[1,0,1,1,0,1,0,1], 'group mean' line, 1/0 labels: correct.

objects.idea: GRPO, Dr. GRPO and RLOO turn the same rewards into different pushes; RLOO is Dr. GRPO times 8/7, and GRPO's length average leaves long wrong replies longer.
objects.image: Three stamps of different sizes pressed on the same lone right answer: one heavy, two nearly alike.

card.title: Three ways to push
card.text: GRPO divides each reply's reward minus the group mean by the group's spread; Dr. GRPO does not divide; RLOO subtracts the mean of the other 7. RLOO is Dr. GRPO times 8/7, and Adam cancels a constant factor, so the two trained alike. GRPO also averages each reply's push over its length, so a long wrong reply is pushed down less per character.
card.formula: GRPO: (rᵢ − mean) / (std + 10⁻⁴)   Dr. GRPO: rᵢ − mean   RLOO: rᵢ − mean of the other 7

card.text: Replace the checker with a coin that hands out as many 1s as the checker would, on wrong replies as often as right ones. Each update then takes a full step in a random direction, and nothing pulls the model back. As it gets worse, more groups score all 0. We expected it to stay near 59.1%; it collapsed.

card.title: Any of k tries
card.text: From n = 128 samples with c right, pass@k is 1 − C(n − c, k) / C(n, k). If training only narrowed the model, the base would win at large k. Here the trained models match or beat the base at every k, but the test had no room: the base was already at 99.56% at k = 16.

also.idea: KL to the base model measures how far training moved the policy.

card.title: How far it moved
card.text: KL to the base is how much more likely the trained model finds its own replies than the base does, on average, in nats per reply. The true-reward runs moved about 1.4 nats and stopped once most groups were all right. The coin-flip runs moved 12.8 and 24.6.

objects.idea: A frozen language model proposes new versions of a short program, a checker scores each one, and the best become the parents of the next.
objects.image: Pots of seedlings where a gardener grafts new shoots onto the strongest plants and pulls the weak ones.

card.title: Evolve programs
card.text: The program is a rule that picks a bin for each item in online bin packing. A 4B model, run on the laptop, is shown two parent rules and asked for a better one. A sandbox runs each child, packs fixed instances and counts the bins against a floor no packing can beat. Rules that score well become parents; the model's weights never change.
card.measured: Kept programs beat best fit by 0.35 ± 0.30 points on held-out instances, in 2 of 3 seeds, at 400 candidates.

Random expression trees, with no model, beat best fit in two seeds of three. With 3 seeds and a spread as large as the gap, evolution did not lose to random search, but did not clearly beat it.

card.title: Without a checker, it drifts
card.text: Accept every child untested and make it the next parent. Asked each time for a better version, in one run the model kept raising its own numbers, a power of 12, then 400, then 10,000, and the scores overflowed early. The other run wrote a rule better than best fit at child 83; the next child replaced it, and that run overflowed too. The model proposes; the checker keeps what works.

card.title: A ruler no plant can reach
card.text: The score is the excess over L1 = ⌈total size / capacity⌉, a floor no packing can beat, so a rule cannot win by losing items or overfilling bins. The parent process packs and checks; the candidate, in a separate process with a screen, time and memory limits and macOS's sandbox, only returns priority(item, bins). Best fit scores 4.781% on the evolve set, first fit 5.340%.

card.title: Does the gain travel?
card.text: Evolution's kept rules gained 0.35 ± 0.30 points on 10 held-out instances, against 0.31 ± 0.31 on the 4 they were chosen on: with 1,000 items per instance there is little to overfit. Random search's seed-0 rule scored 10.71% on uniform sizes in bins of 150, against best fit's 5.01%: it had fit the item sizes, not packing.

objects.idea: A world model predicts what an action will do: here, the agent's next cell on an 8 × 8 grid with walls, so moves can be tried in imagination first.
objects.image: A sand table with an 8 × 8 grid of low walls and one flag; a pawn steps, and a ghost pawn shows where the model thinks it will land.

card.title: Imagine before acting
card.text: Each cell is a wall with chance 0.2; four moves, and a move into a wall leaves the agent where it is. Breadth-first search gives each cell's true distance to the goal. A small network learns to predict the agent's next cell from the grid and the move. Fed its own predictions, it imagines several steps ahead, and its errors pile up.
card.measured: Next cell right 92.5% of the time after one imagined step and 73.9% after eight, against 31.2% and 12.8% for 'did not move'.

objects.idea: Plan by random shooting: imagine many random move sequences, score each by its distance to the goal, take the first move of the best, and plan again.
objects.image: Dozens of ghost pawns race out across the sand; the real pawn takes one step after the best ghost, then the ghosts race again.

card.title: Try many futures, keep one step
card.text: Draw 64 sequences of 8 random moves, imagine each in the model, and score each by its summed distance to the goal over the 8 steps. Take the first move of the best in the real world, then plan again from where you land. Throwing the plan away after one step is called model-predictive control. The score ignores walls, so walls are the model's to handle.
card.measured: Goals reached within 20 steps on 300 test arenas: 75.7% with the learned model, 89.0% with the true world as the model, 3.7% with random moves.

card.title: Low loss, useless latent
card.text: A JEPA predicts the next latent, a compressed code of the grid, instead of the next cell. Its loss fell to 3 × 10⁻⁶, yet a linear probe found no trace of the agent in the latent: it described the arena and dropped the agent, the one thing a move changes. The collapse meters did not flag it, since the latent was spread out, just over the wrong things. Its planner did no better than random moves, and no better than the same model with random weights.

card.title: Two models of it
card.text: Both see the grid and the move and train for 6,000 steps. The one-hot model scores each of the 64 cells and names the next one. The JEPA maps the grid to 32 numbers and predicts the next 32; the target comes from a slow moving average of its encoder, with no gradient. Nothing asks the JEPA to rebuild a cell.

objects.idea: Train a world model end to end from frames with two losses: predict the next embedding, and SIGReg, which keeps the embeddings spread like a standard normal.
objects.image: The picture on the wall is squeezed into a round cloud of marbles that never bunch up.

card.title: Two losses, no shortcut
card.text: An encoder maps each 64 × 64 frame to an embedding; a predictor maps it and a block of 5 moves to the next one. The gradient flows into both sides, with no slow copy and no stop-gradient. SIGReg projects the batch on 1,024 random directions and measures how far each projection is from a standard normal. It is the only thing that stops the encoder from mapping every frame to one point.
card.formula: loss = mse(pred, next z) + 0.1 · SIGReg(z)
card.measured: D = 32, three seeds: normalised std 1.00, effective rank 30.9 of 32, position probe R² 0.77 to 0.89; at D = 192, R² 1.00.

card.title: Narrowing onto noise
card.text: Each planner scores a plan by the distance between the imagined embedding and the goal frame's, takes 5 moves, then plans again. CEM draws 300 plans, keeps the 30 cheapest, refits a Gaussian to them, 10 rounds. But latent distance grows only over the first 30 units of walk, then goes flat, so the 30 cheapest differ by noise. Returning the cheapest plan seen, instead of the final mean, lifted CEM from 26% to 58% (one seed).

objects.idea: A ReLU network cuts its input space into pieces; inside each piece the whole network is one linear map.
objects.image: The map on the table is cut into flat tiles by straight folds, and each tile tilts its own way.

card.title: Pieces, each one linear
card.text: A ReLU neuron is either off (output 0) or on (it passes its input). Fix which neurons are on and the whole network is one linear map; the inputs that share that on/off pattern form a linear region. In 2-D each first-layer neuron switches along one straight line, and each second-layer neuron along one more line inside each piece, so the regions can be cut exactly, polygon by polygon, with no sampling.
card.measured: 158 regions in the square at init, 236 after training to 100% train accuracy: a 2 → 12 → 12 → 2 net on two moons, module 15.

objects.checked: README §1 'Linear regions' (definition, exact cutting, table 158/236); a22/a23 texts against §1 and its width table (21.3, 127.7, 6–40, 40–233, ×1.53/2.09/1.87, 'about 4 per doubling'); formations.js F.relu draws k straight cuts, no captions.

objects.idea: Intrinsic dimension counts the coordinates data needs if you follow its curves; check an estimator on sets of known dimension before trusting it.
objects.image: A ribbon of points curls across the table: it spreads over two dimensions of floor, yet a walker along it needs only one number.

card.title: How much room the data takes
card.text: FashionMNIST images have 784 pixels, but they do not fill 784 dimensions. Two estimators, TwoNN and MLE, read the intrinsic dimension from distances to nearest neighbours alone. On curved cubes of known dimension both land within 1 of the truth, so they can be read on real data. The pixels sit near 13 to 16 dimensions; the trained MLP lowers that at each layer, while the untrained one keeps it at its hidden layer.
card.formula: TwoNN: μ = r₂ / r₁ (2nd over 1st neighbour distance); on a d-dimensional set P(μ > m) = m⁻ᵈ
card.measured: Curved 10-d cube: TwoNN 9.15, MLE 9.06. FashionMNIST pixels 15.69 and 13.14; hidden layer trained 10.21 and 8.47, untrained 15.82 and 13.34: module 15.

objects.checked: README §2 (TwoNN and MLE definitions, known-set table, FashionMNIST table, 'within 1 of the truth', 'pixels sit near a set of 13 to 16'); F.spiral('data') has no captions.

objects.idea: Linear CKA scores how alike two layers are; a high score means something only next to the score of untrained networks.
objects.image: Two maps traced by trained hands match, and two traced by untrained hands match even better, because both just copied the floor.

card.title: Alike, next to what?
card.text: Linear CKA compares whole layers on the same inputs: it is 1 when one is a rotation and rescaling of the other, whatever the order of the neurons. Two trained seeds of module 02's MLP score 0.93 at the hidden layer, though their single neurons match far less well. Two untrained nets score higher still: a random ReLU layer keeps the pixels' shape, so both look like the pixels. Only at the logits does the trained pair stand clearly above the untrained one.
card.formula: CKA(X, Y) = ‖Yᵀ X‖²_F / (‖Xᵀ X‖_F · ‖Yᵀ Y‖_F), columns centred
card.measured: Hidden layer: 0.93 trained pair, 0.95 untrained pair; logits 0.91 against 0.51; untrained hidden layer against the pixels 0.97: FashionMNIST MLP, 5,000 test images, module 15.

also.idea: Count exactly the regions a straight line between two images crosses; the count grows roughly with the number of neurons.
also.image: A string pulled across the map, with a bead at every fold it crosses.

card.title: Count along a line
card.text: In 784 dimensions the regions cannot be drawn, but those a line crosses can be counted exactly: along the line each first-layer neuron switches at most once, at a point you can solve for, and the second layer is linear between those points. Doubling the width multiplied the count by 1.53, 2.09 and 1.87, roughly in step with the neuron count; a count that grew with the product of the widths would multiply by about 4. One seed and 30 lines make it a demo, not a measurement.

also.idea: On curved data PCA needs far more components than the intrinsic dimension: a flat fit pays for every bend.
also.image: A straight ruler laid along the curling ribbon needs many short pieces to follow it.

card.title: A flat fit pays for bends
card.text: PCA finds the flat subspace that holds the most variance. The curved 10-d cube needs 52 components for 90% of its variance and 216 for 99%. FashionMNIST pixels need 83 for 90%, against an intrinsic dimension of 13 to 16.

also.checked: README §3 'PCA against intrinsic dimension' table.

objects.idea: A forward hook reads a module's output while the model runs; return a tensor from it and that tensor replaces the output.
objects.image: A stethoscope pressed to one wire of the running model, and a clamp beside it that can pinch the wire silent.

card.title: Listen, then clamp
card.text: A forward hook is a function PyTorch calls right after a module runs. If it returns nothing it only reads; if it returns a tensor, the rest of the network runs on that edit. In module 04's char-GPT, block 1 neuron 139 tracks spaces closely, yet zeroing it barely moves the loss. A neuron that explains a pattern is not the same as a neuron the model needs.
card.measured: Neuron 139 tracks 'this is a space' at r = 0.967. Loss after a space: 3.046 nats intact, 3.068 with it zeroed, 3.122 with the ten most space-like neurons zeroed: module 11.

objects.idea: A probe trains a straight line to read one fact from one layer's residual stream; a copy with random weights shows what it finds with no learning.
objects.image: A plumb line dropped at each floor of the shaft: low down it hangs among mixed piles, from the eighteenth floor it falls cleanly between two.

card.title: Ask with a straight line
card.text: Feed SST-2 movie-review sentences to SmolLM2-360M, keep the residual vector at the last token after every block, and fit one logistic regression per layer. Accuracy rises in two steps and stays flat from layer 18. The same model with random weights stays flat and low, 58% at best. A probe shows the fact is there in a form a line can read, not that the model uses it.
card.measured: 87.4% at layer 18, best 88.3% at layer 20, against 58.0% at best with random weights; majority class 50.9%: module 11.

objects.idea: Activation patching: paste one activation from a clean run into a corrupt one; if the right answer returns, that place carries the detail.
objects.image: One radio, two broadcasts: carry one wire's signal from the Paris broadcast into the Rome one, and Paris comes back.

card.title: Swap a piece and watch
card.text: The clean prompt 'The Eiffel Tower is located in the city of' ends in Paris; the corrupt one, with 'The Colosseum', ends in Rome. Rerun the corrupt prompt 330 times, each time pasting one clean vector at one layer and one position. The model holds the landmark on its own tokens for most of its depth, and moves it to the last token at layer 27. Pasting clean into corrupt asks whether a cell is enough; the reverse asks whether it is needed.
card.measured: Patching 'iffel' at layer 3 restored 0.919 of the answer; the last token restored at most 0.11 up to layer 26, then 0.792 at layer 27: SmolLM2-360M, module 11.

objects.checked: README §3 (prompts, 330 runs, metric, two places, layer 27, enough versus needed); a54 against §3.

objects.idea: Who feeds a neuron is an exact sum of earlier writes; who reads it is only an estimate, so check it by zeroing the neuron.
objects.image: Threads from lower floors tie onto one bell, each tagged with a share that adds up exactly; threads to higher floors are guesses until you silence the bell.

card.title: Who feeds it, who reads it
card.text: The residual stream is a plain sum: the token embedding, every attention output, and every earlier neuron's write. Hold RMSNorm's divisor at its actual value and a neuron's gate and up inputs split into one term per write, and the terms add up to the model's own value. Going forward, a first-order estimate of each later neuron's change is often wrong, so zero the neuron, rerun, and compare.
card.measured: Splits match the model's value to about 10⁻⁶. Reader estimates: median error 20% in the next layer, 114% further on, 4 of 20 with the wrong sign. L4/N2177 of SmolLM2-360M, module 11.

objects.checked: README §5 (sum of writes, RMSNorm held, identity checked, forward estimate, printed output, 'Four things to read off it'); F.graph has no captions.

also.idea: Read an MLP neuron by its top contexts on both poles, positive and negative; three neurons prove nothing about the rest.
also.image: A bell that rings one tune when pushed and another when pulled.

card.title: Two poles per neuron
card.text: In SmolLM2's gated MLP a neuron's value is silu(gate) × up, so it can be large and positive or large and negative: two poles. Three neurons drawn at random were read by their ten strongest contexts on each sign. Some poles look like one job, others like a mix: in L28/N1308 the positive pole is a mix and the negative pole reads cleanly, so reading one side alone would miss it. Three neurons and one reader's eye make this a demo.

objects.idea: When features are rare, a small model can store more of them than it has dimensions by sharing directions; whether trained models do this is open.
objects.image: Five weathervanes crammed in a pentagon onto a roof built for two; they seldom turn at once, so they rarely clash.

card.title: More features than dimensions
card.text: The toy squeezes n features into m < n dimensions and reads them back through a ReLU. With dense features it keeps exactly m, each on its own axis. As features get rarer it keeps more, sharing directions, and the ReLU clips most of the crosstalk because two rare features seldom fire together. It is a toy with made-up, independent features: it says nothing about whether trained language models do this.
card.formula: h = W x;  x′ = ReLU(Wᵀ h + b);  loss = Σᵢ Iᵢ (xᵢ − x′ᵢ)²
card.measured: Features kept rose from 5 to 13 of 20, in 5 dimensions, as sparsity went from 0 to 0.999; 5 features in 2 dimensions lie as a pentagon at 0.999: module 12.

objects.checked: README §1 (model, kept rule, table A and B, pentagon, 'What this shows, and what it does not'); a50, a51 against §1; F.superpos caption '2 dimensions · 5 features' matches setup B.

objects.idea: A TopK sparse autoencoder rewrites each activation as a few directions from a long dictionary, then rebuilds the activation from them.
objects.image: A wall of 2,048 small drawers; for each character the model reads, 32 light up, and together they spell its state.

card.title: Read it with a dictionary
card.text: A sparse autoencoder maps an activation to a wide, mostly zero code, then rebuilds the activation from it. TopK keeps the k largest values and zeroes the rest, so k sets how many latents fire. Each latent, one entry of the code, is hoped to fire for one thing. The dictionary is not a fixed fact about the model: on a far larger model, a published test found that two SAEs differing only in seed shared about 30% of their features.
card.formula: z = TopK(ReLU(W_enc·(x − b_pre) + b_enc));  x′ = W_dec·z + b_pre
card.measured: k = 32 of 2,048 latents explained 98.7% of the variance and closed 98.4% of the loss gap: block 1 MLP of module 04's char-GPT, module 12.

objects.checked: README §2 (formula, latent, Paulo and Belrose, TopK, metrics table); a52 against §2; F.dict lights about a tenth of 42 rays, no captions.

objects.idea: A steering vector is a direction added to the model's state as it writes; replies lean that way, and a sentiment score alone cannot judge them.
objects.image: A finger pushes the weathervane toward 'glad': the talk turns cheerful, and at a harder push it wanders off the question.

card.title: Push along a direction
card.text: The plainest steering vector is the mean state on eight positive sentences minus the mean on eight negative ones, added at layer 16 of SmolLM2-360M-Instruct at every position. A random direction of the same size is the control, and a one-line system prompt the rival. At ×4 the score reads 1.00, yet three of four replies left the request. Four requests make this a demo, not a measurement.
card.measured: Mean P(positive) 0.52 plain, 0.81 at ×2, 1.00 at ×4, 0.38 for a random direction, 0.996 for the prompt 'Reply in an upbeat tone.': module 12.

objects.checked: README §4 (vector, layer 16, norm, five conditions, table, what the four show, demo caveat); a55 against §4.

also.idea: Measure an SAE by variance explained, L0, dead latents, and the loss when its rebuild replaces the layer.
also.image: Four dials on the drawer wall; one counts drawers no one ever opens.

card.title: Four dials for an SAE
card.text: Variance explained says how well the SAE rebuilds the layer; L0, the latents active per input, is fixed at k by TopK. A dead latent never fires on held-out text. The strongest test splices the rebuild into the model and measures the next-character loss. At k = 32: 98.7% of variance, 274 of 2,048 latents dead, loss 1.729 nats against 1.724 intact and 2.042 with the neurons replaced by their mean.

also.checked: README §2 metrics table and the paragraph below it.

also.idea: Neurons beat random directions when a layer may pass on only k numbers, but an untrained copy and a GELU null show how much of that edge needs no learning.
also.image: Three scales weigh what eight kept numbers carry: an untrained copy tips a little, GELU noise tips most of the way, the trained model only a bit further.

card.title: Neurons, against a null
card.text: Top-k keeps a layer's k entries largest in size, sign ignored, and zeroes the rest, either in the neuron basis or after a fixed random rotation. At k = 8, eight neurons do in loss what about 33 random directions do. But GELU acts on each neuron alone, which makes its own axes special whether or not anything was learned. Against a GELU null, learning adds only 1.47×.
card.formula: neurons: h_k = TopK(h);  random: h_k = TopK(h Q) Qᵀ
card.measured: Output kept, exchange rate at k = 8: untrained copy 1.84×, GELU null 4.24×, trained 6.23×; loss exchange rate 4.16×: module 04's char-GPT, module 12.

also.checked: README §5 (top-k, exchange rate, controls, table, 'needs a null'); vbars spec uses the table's numbers.

objects.idea: A claim about one unit needs other image sets and a rank among neighbouring units; InceptionV1 channel 4e:55 ranked last of 21 as a V detector.
objects.image: Twenty-one lenses hang from one rail, each lower the more the photos beat the drawn Vs for it; none rises above the rail, and the lens called 'V' hangs lowest of all.

card.title: One unit needs neighbours
card.text: Channel 55 of InceptionV1's layer 4e has been read as a V-shape unit. Read with a forward hook before the ReLU on 200 drawn Vs, Os, cats, cars, garbage trucks and other photos, it responds to cats more than ten times harder than to Vs. Among channels 45 to 65 its gap between Vs and photos is the most negative, and a copy with random weights shows a gap too. The run fails this test of the V reading but does not refute it: flat drawings hardly drive any channel at this depth.
card.measured: Median of 4e:55: drawn V 68.0, drawn O 34.8, cats 798.2, CIFAR cars 194.6. Gap −3.48, rank 21 of 21; random weights −1.06: module 13.

objects.checked: README §1 (method, set table, gap definition, rank table, random control, 'What the miss does and does not show'); the hanging lenses drawn from results/v_neuron.json, gap_by_channel 45 to 65.

objects.idea: Probe a vision transformer block by block for the class, against the same network with random weights.
objects.image: Plumb lines down the twelve floors of a glass tower read the class more plainly at each floor; in a tower of random glass beside it they barely do.

card.title: A probe per block
card.text: CLIP ViT-B/32 cuts an image into 7 × 7 patches, adds one CLS token and runs 12 blocks. One logistic regression per block reads the imagenette class from the CLS vector. The trained curve climbs at every block. The random-weight copy stays low, but above chance: random attention still mixes a little patch content into CLS.
card.measured: Held-out accuracy 32.4% after block 1, 78.2% after block 4, 98.0% after block 12; random weights 33.6% at best; chance 10%: module 13.

objects.checked: README §3 'A class probe per block' (setup, table, random 24.6%–33.6% explanation).

objects.idea: Probe a frozen JEPA encoder for what it keeps; a negative R² means the probe does worse than guessing the mean.
objects.image: A telescope at the window reads the yard's tile world: it finds where the agent stands, but its guess of how far the goal lies falls below a plain average.

card.title: What a JEPA latent holds
card.text: A JEPA learns by predicting the latent of the next observation, never its pixels. Freeze gridjepa's encoder, which maps a 15 × 15 window of a tile world to 128 numbers, and fit linear probes on arenas it never saw. Position and the neighbouring tiles read well, but random encoders come close. For path length to the goal every R² is below zero, the raw window's included; a likely reason is that 97 arenas are too few for the probe to carry over.
card.formula: R² = 1 − (probe's squared error) / (squared error of always guessing the mean)
card.measured: Position R² 0.983 trained, 0.944–0.960 random; neighbours 97.4% against 86.6%–89.8%; path length −0.347 trained, −0.210 to −0.218 random, −0.629 raw window: module 13.

objects.checked: README §4 (JEPA, encoder, split, three probes, controls, table, 'What went wrong, read after the fact'); random seed 0 values in the vbars spec.
