also.idea: Feature visualisation paints the image that drives one channel hardest; it is one picture the optimiser found, not a measurement.
also.image: A painter who paints only what makes one lens glow, and the canvas fills with cat faces.

card.title: Paint what a channel wants
card.text: Start from noise and take 512 gradient steps on the pixels to raise one channel's mean value, with small random shifts, scales and rotations at each step. The 4e:55 render shows cat faces, which matches the cat result, but it is one image, not a measure of what the channel does. Renders reach two to three times the best real image: 3634.8 against 1788.1 for 4e:55.

also.checked: README §2 (method, table, reading by eye, ratio).

also.idea: Read a neuron by its top images, and know that three neurons prove nothing about the rest.
also.image: Three portraits of three neurons' favourite photos, and a sign underneath: 'three of 36,864'.

card.title: Three neurons prove nothing
card.text: Draw one neuron at random in blocks 3, 7 and 11 of CLIP, score 1,500 images by its largest value over the 49 patches, and look at the top eight. One reads as mixed, one as mostly boxy machines, one as chain saws and people holding a tool or a fish. Imagenette has only ten classes, so the top images come from those ten whatever the neuron responds to.

also.checked: README §3 'Three neurons drawn at random' (table, 36,861 others, ten-class caveat).

objects.idea: Build a model whose units you know, then grade each tool by how many of those units it finds.
objects.image: A clock with its gears behind glass: you know every wheel, so you can check the repairman's list against it.

card.title: Grade the tool on known answers
card.text: Each MLP of a two-block model keeps only 8 of its 2,048 neurons per token, so those neurons are the units it computes with. Fit an SAE and a transcoder to block 1's MLP. For each true neuron take the best cosine between its value vector and any dictionary column; a neuron counts as recovered at 0.9 or more. Here the SAE won, the reverse of the paper this copies.
card.formula: MMCS = mean over true neurons i of maxⱼ cos(vᵢ, dⱼ)
card.measured: SAE: MMCS 0.802, 63.0% of neurons recovered; transcoder 0.625, 34.9%; 2,048 random directions give 0.30: TinyStories, three seeds, module 32.

objects.checked: README §1 (model, 8 of 2,048), §2 (dictionaries, MMCS, recovered, table, reversal), exercise (a) 0.30; a58 against §1–2; F.truth caption '5 of 8 found' (62.5%) agrees with the SAE's 63.0%.

objects.idea: Run the same tools on a copy with random weights: here the dictionaries found its units as well as the trained model's.
objects.image: A second clock of random parts on the lookout ledge, and the repairman lists its gears just as neatly.

card.title: Would a random network do the same?
card.text: The random copy keeps the same gate, so it has true neurons too. The dictionaries recover them as well as the trained model's: matching a model's units says nothing about whether it learned, only that the layer is sparse in some basis. The detection score did tell trained from random here, unlike the published result.
card.measured: SAE MMCS 0.840 on the random copy, 0.802 on the trained model; transcoder 0.627 against 0.625; detection of SAE latents 0.60 against 0.80: module 32.

objects.checked: README §3 (control, table, three readings); a56 against §3; F.panels('reveal') ends on '≈' between trained and random, which fits MMCS.

objects.idea: An attribution graph scores each neuron by activation times gradient in a frozen model; test it by zeroing neurons in the real one.
objects.image: A map of which gears drive the clock's hands; pull one gear and see whether the hands stop.

card.title: Attribute, then ablate
card.text: Freeze the attention patterns, the LayerNorm scales and which 8 neurons each gate keeps. The target logit is then linear in every neuron's activation, so activation × gradient equals the drop when that neuron is zeroed, as long as no kept neuron's input crosses zero. Then zero each neuron in the real model, with nothing frozen, and compare. On the random copy attribution fails, yet keeping its top 20 neurons still scores 0.99: a faithfulness ratio near 1 means little unless removing everything moves the answer.
card.measured: Attribution against real drop: r = 0.88 on the trained model, 0.42 on the random copy; the top 10 beat 10 random neurons on 20 of 20 prompts; the top 20 keep 0.96 of P(target): module 32.

objects.checked: README §5 (steps 1–4, table, faithfulness, random copy); F.graph has no captions.

also.idea: Score a dictionary against the truth by MMCS: the mean, over true neurons, of the best cosine with any dictionary column.
also.image: Each true gear is held up to every found gear and scored by its closest fit.

card.title: Best cosine, averaged
card.text: For each alive true neuron, MMCS takes the highest cosine between its value vector and any decoder column, then averages. 2,048 random directions in 128 dimensions give 0.30. Even the better dictionary finds about two neurons in three; most of the rest sit near chance, with no latent for them at all.

also.checked: README §2 (MMCS, 0.30, 'What a dictionary misses').

also.idea: Match two seeds' dictionaries one to one; here a latent that matched a true neuron nearly always came back in the second seed, and one that matched none never did.
also.image: Two telescopes on two towers tick off the stars both see, nearly every real star is on both lists, and no plainly false one is.

card.title: Train twice, trust what returns
card.text: Pair the decoder columns of two seeds one to one, maximising the summed cosine (the Hungarian method); a latent is shared when its partner sits at cosine 0.7 or more. On the trained model, an SAE latent that matches a true neuron came back 95 times in 100, one that matches none never did. With no ground truth this is a cheap check, but it cannot tell a learned unit from a random model's.

also.checked: README §4 (matching, 0.7 threshold, table 79.3%, 94.5%, 0.0%, 'Seed agreement tracks the truth').

route.why: Start at the far end of the old garden, at a line strung between two stakes: the perceptron moves its line each time it is wrong, and least squares finds the line closest to every point.
Next door grow four older tricks that learn with no gradient: count with Bayes, ask the neighbours, find the main axis, sum a cloud up with a few centres.

The string line stopped at the first cut that worked. The pond finds the widest one, lifts points so a flat cut works, keeps memories as hollows, and shows the curve that dips twice. Its outflow runs to attention, in the house.
Down the garden steps, the echo room: every sum you compute leaves a stone joined to its inputs, and the slope echoes back through the stones, one local slope at a time.
Slopes alone train nothing: the mill turns them into a loop of batches, steps and measures, and shows the loss on unseen data turning up.
Unseen data has to stay unseen: beside the mill sits the vault, where splits, counts, thresholds and leaks are kept honest.
The floor sinks into a slope. Watch how the optimiser moves down it, how step size and momentum change the path, and how the right answer can come long after the fit.
Every room so far learned from labels. Here the data supplies its own targets: hide part and predict it, or match two views, and stop the cheat where every input maps to one point.
Last room on the gradient's path: what if nothing is sent back through the whole network? Learning with forward passes and local goals, and what each way costs.
Text arrives at the west gate and is chopped into tokens by a fixed list of merges. From here the walk turns into the stair core and runs east down the corridor where the blue stream starts.
You met the blue stream at its source in the corridor, where each token became a vector: its token embedding plus its position. In the atrium each token asks the tokens before it what to read.
Pictures skip the gate's merges: cut into patches at the south door, they walk into the same block, and nobody wears blinkers.
At the end of the row stands a real model, SmolLM2-360M, thirty-two blocks deep; its last 960-number vector becomes odds over all 49,152 tokens, read on the balcony.
From the balcony, turn back along the north row: the scriptorium writes one token at a time, keeps each token's keys and values, and sends it back to the gate.
The scriptorium's shelves grow with every token; the satchel room carries a fixed-size state instead.
A fixed state can be a matrix that stores values under keys: the slate room compares four ways to write it, from plain adding to correcting what the slate already returns.
Every room so far wrote one token after another. The fog room makes a whole picture at once, by removing noise step by step.
Bring that idea back to text: start from a line of blanks and fill in a few at a time, in any order. The stair core is next door.
You have seen the whole model. Before climbing, go down below the cellar to the footings: how loss falls with size, and how big to build for a budget.
Up to the first floor, where weights change after training: the tailor refits a trained model by training two thin matrices beside each frozen one.
Every fitting costs something: on the fading shelf the old skill wears away while the new one is learned.
Instead of showing good replies, show two and say which is better: the tasting room learns from choices.
A tuned model is still big: the press makes it smaller by teaching, cutting and rounding.
The press rounded after training; the three-coin room trains with three values from the start, and rounds the cache too.
Up again: from here on no weight moves. At the example desk a frozen model learns a rule from examples in its prompt.
Examples help; spending more tokens helps too: the scratch room thinks out loud and takes a vote.
If words change the answer, tune the words: the sign-painter repaints the instruction and keeps what scores.
Some answers are not in the weights at all: the library fetches the best-matching page and pastes it into the prompt.
Give the model tools and a loop: the workshop of hands acts, reads the result and acts again. Its door opens on the outside stair.
Down in the yard the world gives scores, not labels: pull levers, keep what pays, and do not move too fast.
Put a language model in the yard and let a program mark its answers: reward from a checker.
Keep the checker, freeze the model: the greenhouse breeds programs and keeps only what the checker passes.
Instead of trying moves in the world, try them in a model of it: the sand table plans before acting.
Build that model from pictures alone: the camera obscura plans inside what it learned from frames. Its back wall is the tower.
Climb to look inside. At the tower's foot, the map room shows the shapes inside a network: the pieces a ReLU net cuts, the room its data takes, and whether two nets hold the same shape.
One floor up, listen to single parts of a running model: hooks, probes, patches, neurons and their wiring.
Do single neurons each hold one thing? The dictionary room rewrites each state as a few directions from a long list, then tests neurons against random directions.
Point the same tools at vision models and a small world model, and ask what one unit or one probe can prove.
At the top, test every finding against a random copy, a second seed and a known truth. From the lookout the whole palace lies below: walk it again in your head.

landmarks.what: A channel of blue water down the ground-floor corridor from the gate to the balcony. Every ground-floor room has a door on it and pours in; from any room you can see it.
Directly below, in the cellar, a channel of gold water runs the other way, west. Grates in the ground-floor corridor show it.
The output balcony looks east over the old garden: you can see the string-line bed where the walk began, farthest away because it is oldest.
Steps from the garden go down under the balcony into the cellar: the loss is computed at the output, so learning starts beneath it.
The stair core stands beside the gate. The cellar stair comes up there because the gradient reaches the embedding table last; every upper floor is reached from where text enters.
The picture door opens south onto the yard path: images come from the world and skip the gate's merges: they are cut into patches instead.
A light well in the yard path looks down into the blindfold room (16): the JEPA objective below, the JEPA world models (25, 31) across the path.
The tailor's room floor is glass over the atrium: thin matrices are added above the frozen block.

The north row is one storey high with a skylight roof; from the first-floor gallery outside the three-coin room you look down through the skylight onto the scriptorium's KV shelves (07), which 28 also rounds.
The only way from the house's top floor to the yard is the outside stair from the workshop of hands: agents are where the model starts to act.
The tower stands at the south-west corner and is the tallest thing. From the lookout you see the whole roof, the yard and, far east, the garden: the place to rehearse the walk.

prologue.what: Before the first bower, the garden gate: 420 points in a loose field (a1), then a grid of numbers (a2), then two kinds of points and a first wrong line (a3, a4). It opens the walk the way the Moves page opens.

epilogue.what: At the top, the Moves page's last chapter: five ideas that kept coming back, each pointing at rooms below: hide and predict (16, 33), one local rule (01), lookup as a dot product (04, 21, 27), propose, score, keep (22, 34, 35), no number without its control (05a, 32).
